course.title: Economics: Markets and Strategy
course.description: Price a trade-off, find where supply meets demand, weigh a tax and outguess a rival. Every idea is worked with real numbers.
course.audience: An adult comfortable with basic algebra: solving two linear equations and finding the area of a triangle. No previous economics is assumed; the depth matches a strong first-year university microeconomics course.

paragraphs: An hour can be spent only once, and so can a pound, a field of wheat or a week of a workshop's time. Economics is the study of choice when there isn't enough of these to go round, and it starts from the observation that every choice gives something up. Once we count that cost in the things given up, and not only in money, choices that seem to have nothing in common, such as a student's evening, a workshop's week and a country's harvest, can be weighed against each other in the same terms.

Most of the prices you pay are set by nobody in particular. Thousands of buyers and sellers each make their own plans, and the price of coffee or of a concert ticket settles where those plans fit together, then moves when something changes them, such as a frost, a new fashion or a tax. Economists write each side's plans as a short equation, and with two such equations and a little algebra we can say where a price will settle, who gains from the sales that happen, and what a tax or a cap on the price takes away.

The same reasoning reaches beyond markets with many sellers. A firm that is the only seller of something, or two firms each choosing a price while watching the other, makes choices whose results depend on what someone else does, and economics gives us a way to work out what each is likely to do without guessing at anyone's motives. Because every step is worked with numbers you can check, you can see exactly where an argument about prices or policy stands or falls.
outcomes: You'll be able to price a choice by what it gives up, and say who should make what.
You'll be able to read demand and supply equations and solve them for the price where a market settles.
You'll be able to work out how a tax, a price control or a shift in buyers' wants changes a market.
You'll be able to find the output and price that maximise a firm's profit.
You'll be able to find the likely outcome of a simple strategic game between two players.
introduction.prerequisites: You should be comfortable with basic algebra, such as solving 100 − 2P = 4P − 20, and with finding the area of a triangle.

concepts.title: What it really costs
concepts.summary: Measure opportunity cost along a production possibilities frontier, and see why it usually rises.

concepts.title: Who should make what
concepts.summary: Find comparative advantage from opportunity costs and show that specialisation and trade benefit both sides.

concepts.title: The next unit
concepts.summary: Choose how much of an activity to do by comparing marginal benefit with marginal cost, and ignore sunk costs.

concepts.title: Demand meets supply
concepts.summary: Read linear demand and supply equations and solve them for the equilibrium price and quantity.

concepts.title: When the curves move
concepts.summary: Separate movements along a curve from shifts of it, and solve for the new equilibrium after a shift.

concepts.title: How strongly buyers respond
concepts.summary: Measure price elasticity of demand with the midpoint method and predict what a price change does to revenue.

concepts.title: Who gains from a sale
concepts.summary: Measure consumer and producer surplus as areas on the diagram and see why equilibrium makes their total largest.

concepts.title: What a tax takes
concepts.summary: Work out what a per-unit tax does to prices and revenue. Then measure the surplus it destroys and find who bears it.

concepts.title: Controls and spillovers
concepts.summary: Predict shortages and surpluses from price controls, and correct an external cost with a Pigouvian tax.

concepts.title: Costs and the best output
concepts.summary: Separate fixed, variable, average and marginal cost, and choose output where marginal revenue equals marginal cost.

concepts.title: One seller
concepts.summary: Derive a single seller's marginal revenue and use it to find its price and output. Then measure the deadweight loss of monopoly.

concepts.title: Strategic choices
concepts.summary: Find best responses, dominant strategies and Nash equilibria in payoff matrices, and see how repetition supports cooperation.

lessons.title: What it really costs

steps.headline: The real cost of a choice is the best thing you give up

lead.text: The sum you have just done priced a ticket in sandwiches rather than in pounds, and that small change of units is the idea this whole course is built on. Money is limited, so whenever you spend it on one thing you quietly decide not to spend it on another, and the price tag records only the first half of that decision. What you passed over is the other half, and we call it the **opportunity cost** of the choice: the value of the *best* alternative you gave up.

The figure shows a £20 afternoon as five £4 blocks. Spend it all on bubble tea and you have five teas. Put £8 into a paperback and the same £8 would have bought two teas, so the book's opportunity cost is two teas, and three are all that remain. We say the best alternative because you could only have done one of the other things. If £8 could have bought two teas or a snack you'd have enjoyed less, the cost is the teas, and not the teas and the snack added together.

Time works in exactly the same way, and it is often the scarcer of the two. An hour spent reading is an hour not spent on anything else, so its cost is the best use of that hour you gave up, whatever that use would have paid. Because **the cost is measured in what you forgo**, we can count it in any units we like, and that is what lets us price the choices of a workshop or a whole country over the next few screens.

steps.headline: Divide the two maximums to price one good in the other

lead.text: Now put a workshop in place of a wallet. Suppose Workshop B can spend a whole week building chairs and finish 40 of them, or spend the same week building tables and finish 20. It can't do both with the same hours, so every table it builds costs it chairs, and the figure draws the two extreme weeks as the ends of a line. How many chairs is one table worth? Twenty tables take the whole week that 40 chairs would, so one table takes a twentieth of the week, and a twentieth of the week could have made 40 ÷ 20 = 2 chairs. That is the rule: **the opportunity cost of one table is the most chairs divided by the most tables**.

Workshop C, in the second view, can make at most 50 chairs or 10 tables. Its tables are slow to build, and the same division shows it: 50 ÷ 10 = 5 chairs for every table. Both workshops make tables, but a table displaces two chairs in one and five in the other.

afterFigure.text: Turn the sum upside down and you price chairs in tables. Workshop B gives up 20 ÷ 40 = half a table for every chair, and the two prices are *reciprocals* of each other, because they describe the same trade-off read from opposite ends.

steps.headline: The frontier shows every week the workshop could manage

lead.text: So far we have looked only at the two extreme weeks, but a workshop can also split its time. Spend half the week on each and Workshop B makes 20 chairs and 10 tables, which is the marked point on its line; Workshop C, splitting its week the same way, makes 25 chairs and 5 tables. Every split lands somewhere on the straight line joining the two extremes, and we call that line the **production possibilities frontier**, because it marks the edge of what the workshop can make with the time it has.

afterFigure.text: Where a point sits relative to that edge tells you something. A point *on* the frontier uses the whole week. A point *inside* it, such as 20 chairs and 5 tables for Workshop B, leaves time unused, so the workshop could have made more of something without making less of anything else. And a point *beyond* the frontier would need more hours than the week contains, so no use of these resources can reach it.

steps.headline: On a real frontier, each step along it has its own price

lead.text: Real economies don't swap one good for another at a steady rate, so their frontiers are rarely straight lines. Take a country that can make food or machines. Its frontier runs from 100 machines and no food at one end to 80 units of food and no machines at the other, and the figure marks two points along the way, at 20 and 40 units of food. Its frontier runs from 100 machines and no food at one end to 80 units of food and no machines at the other, with a point marked every 20 units of food, and the figure shows its first stretch, up to 40 units of food. The price of moving from one point to the next is **what you lose of one good divided by what you gain of the other**, and you work it out *one step at a time*.

Take the first step, from no food to 20 units. Machines fall from 100 to 90, so 10 machines are given up for 20 units of food, which is 10 ÷ 20 = 0.5 machines for each unit. Hold that number in mind and switch to the straight frontier in the second view, where the price is the same everywhere: 100 ÷ 80 = 1.25 machines per unit of food.

afterFigure.text: The straight line has one price from end to end. The bowed one, as the next steps will show, does not.

steps.headline: Pricing the step from 40 food to 60 food

lead.text: The same method applies to any step. Here it is for the third step on the bowed frontier, with two of the readings left for you to do.

workedSteps.text: Read the machines at 40 units of food from the frontier.
Read the machines at 60 units of food.
Subtract to find the machines given up.
Food rises from 40 to 60, so the food gained is 60 − 40.
Divide the machines given up by the food gained.

steps.headline: On a bowed frontier each extra unit costs more than the last

lead.text: Put the four step prices side by side: 0.5, 1, 1.5 and 2 machines for each unit of food. Every unit of food now costs more machines than the one before it, which is exactly why the frontier bows outward and doesn't run straight. We call this **increasing opportunity cost**, and it is the normal case rather than the exception.

Why should it happen? Because land, workers and machinery are not equally good at everything. When the country first turns towards food, it moves the resources best suited to growing it, such as fertile land, and gives up few machines. As it asks for more food it has to draw in resources that are far better at making machines than at farming, so each further unit costs more machines. If every resource were equally suited to both jobs, the frontier would be straight, as in the second view, and every unit would cost the same.

afterFigure.text: The rule holds from either end. The more machines the country already makes, the more food each additional machine costs it, so a country pays most for the last bit of whatever it is already making a lot of.

lead.text: Nothing here depends on workshops or countries, and a fixed block of study time is a frontier too.

lessons.orientation: Measure opportunity cost along a production possibilities frontier, and see why it usually rises.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: What does a £10 cinema ticket cost? The price tag says £10, and that is certainly what leaves your pocket, but it is only the money. An economist would ask a different question: what else could that £10 have done? Money and time can each be spent only once, so every purchase quietly rules something out, and the cost that matters is the thing ruled out.

That sounds like a quibble until you try to compare choices that have nothing in common, such as a film, a day's work and a new factory. Their money prices can't tell you which is dearer, but counting what each one gives up can, and the same counting tells a workshop how many chairs each table costs it, or a country how many machines it gives up for each extra unit of food.

intro.promise: By the end you'll price a choice by what it gives up, and read the cost of each extra unit from a production possibilities frontier.

recap.keyIdea: A choice costs the best alternative it gives up, and along a frontier that cost is what you lose of one good for each unit you gain of the other.

blocks.text: **Opportunity cost** is what you give up, counted in the thing you gave up, so a ticket costs two sandwiches and a table costs three chairs. On a [[production possibilities frontier|The line showing every combination of two goods that a fixed set of resources can make. Met in 'What it really costs'.]] you find the price of a step by dividing what you lose of one good by what you gain of the other, and when the frontier bows outward that price *rises* with every step.

recap.nextHook: Different producers face different costs, which raises the question of who should make what.

lessons.title: Who should make what

steps.headline: A producer's two prices are one trade-off read from each end

lead.text: Before comparing two people we need each person's prices. A potter can fill a day with 9 bowls or with 3 vases, so a vase takes the time of three bowls, and making one means giving up 9 ÷ 3 = 3 bowls. That is the potter's [[opportunity cost|The value of the best alternative given up, counted in the thing given up. Met in 'What it really costs'.]] of a vase. The bowl has a price of its own, found by turning the sum over: a bowl takes a third of a vase's time, so it costs 3 ÷ 9 = a third of a vase.

afterFigure.text: These are **one trade-off read from opposite ends**, which is why each price is the *reciprocal* of the other. That fact does a lot of work in what follows: if a producer's vase is cheap in bowls, then its bowl is dear in vases, and the reverse.

steps.headline: A producer has a comparative advantage in the good it gives up least to make

lead.text: Now compare two potters. Mo can make 3 vases or 9 bowls in a day, and Jo can make 2 vases or 4 bowls. Mo is simply better, since he makes more vases *and* more bowls, and we say he has an **absolute advantage** in both, meaning he can produce more of a good with the same time. If speed were all that mattered, Jo would have nothing to offer him.

Price the goods instead. A vase costs Mo 9 ÷ 3 = 3 bowls and costs Jo 4 ÷ 2 = 2 bowls, so Jo gives up fewer bowls for each vase he makes. Turn it over and a bowl costs Mo a third of a vase but costs Jo half of one, so Mo gives up less to make a bowl. We say a producer has a **comparative advantage** in a good when its opportunity cost of that good is *lower* than the other producer's. Jo has it in vases and Mo has it in bowls, however much better Mo is at both.

afterFigure.text: David Ricardo set the idea out in 1817, using English cloth and Portuguese wine. Whenever two producers' prices differ, as they do here, each has a comparative advantage in exactly one of the two goods, so nobody is left with nothing to offer. The second view, Ola and Pat, shows it again with different numbers.

steps.headline: Who should bake what, Ana or Ben?

lead.text: The method is to price both goods for both bakers and let the lower price decide, one good at a time.

workedSteps.text: Price a cake in loaves for each baker by dividing loaves by cakes.
Ben gives up fewer loaves, so Ben has the comparative advantage in cakes.
Now price a loaf in cakes, the other way up.
workedSteps.math: Ana: 6 ÷ 12 = 0.5 cake. Ben: 4 ÷ 6 = 2/3 of a cake.

workedSteps.text: So Ana should bake the loaves and Ben the cakes.

steps.headline: Each does the job they are cheaper at, then they swap

lead.text: Let each potter do what he gives up least to do: Jo makes vases, Mo makes bowls, and they swap. Suppose Mo pays Jo 2.5 bowls for a vase. A vase costs Jo 2 bowls to make, so he receives 2.5 bowls for something that cost him 2, and he is half a bowl ahead. Making the vase himself would have cost Mo 3 bowls, so paying 2.5 saves him half a bowl. The trade works because of the gap between 2 and 3: each potter is **buying a good at a lower price than he could make it for**.

afterFigure.text: You can check that nothing was conjured up. If each potter simply split his day in half, the two together would make 2.5 vases and 6.5 bowls. If Jo makes only vases, which is 2 of them, and Mo makes the other half vase and spends the rest of his day on bowls, they make the same 2.5 vases and 7.5 bowls, one bowl more, and that extra bowl is the half-bowl each of them gained.

steps.headline: Any price between the two costs makes both better off

lead.text: Why 2.5? Because it sits between 2 and 3. Jo will sell a vase only for more than the 2 bowls it costs him to make, and Mo will buy only at less than the 3 bowls it would cost him, so **any price between the two costs** works. The nearer it sits to one end, the more of the gain goes to the potter at the other end. Use the buttons to try a price below that range, inside it and above it.

afterFigure.text: Where in the range the price lands is a matter of bargaining, and economics alone does not settle it. What economics settles is that a deal is *possible* at all, and that outside the range one side is better off staying out.

steps.headline: Ben and Ana swap at 1.75 loaves a cake

lead.text: Back to the bakers. Ben's cake costs him 1.5 loaves and Ana's costs her 2, so a price of 1.75 sits between the two, and Ben will bake cakes for Ana. Work through what Ben gains, filling in the lines marked for you.

workedSteps.text: Ben bakes cakes all day and sells 2 of them to Ana at 1.75 loaves each. How many loaves does he receive?
Without the swap, 2 cakes would have used half his day, leaving time for 3 loaves. With it he still has 2 cakes, plus the loaves he received.
Compare the two.

steps.headline: Trade gains come from a difference in costs

lead.text: Look back at what powered every swap in this lesson: a gap between two prices. Jo and Mo gained because a vase cost one of them 2 bowls and the other 3, and Ana and Ben because a cake cost 2 loaves and 1.5. Nothing in the reasoning depended on *who was faster*.

Now suppose two bakers give up exactly the same number of loaves for each cake. Whatever price one of them would accept for a cake, the other could match by baking it, so there is no price at which buying beats making, and no gain to share. **Comparative advantage exists only when the costs differ**.

lessons.orientation: Find comparative advantage from opportunity costs and show that specialisation and trade benefit both sides.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: Suppose one baker is quicker than another at everything, turning out more loaves in a day and more cakes as well. It looks as though she has no reason to buy anything from the slower baker, since she could make it herself in less time, and yet trade between the two can leave *both* of them better off.

What makes that possible is that the two bakers give up different amounts of bread to make a cake, and those amounts, their opportunity costs from the last lesson, matter more than which of them works faster. Comparing them tells you which of two producers should make which good, whether they are bakers, potters or whole countries, and at what price a swap pays both sides.

intro.promise: By the end you'll decide who should make what by comparing opportunity costs, and show that a swap at the right price leaves both sides better off.

recap.keyIdea: Each producer should make the good it gives up least to make, and a swap at a price between the two costs leaves both better off.

blocks.text: A producer has a **comparative advantage** in a good when its opportunity cost of that good is lower, and you find it by pricing each good in the other for both producers and comparing. If each makes the good it is cheaper at and they swap at a price between the two costs, both end up with more than they could make alone, whereas two producers with *identical* costs have nothing to gain.

recap.nextHook: So far we've compared whole choices; the next lesson asks how to decide one extra unit at a time.

lessons.title: The next unit

steps.headline: Keep going while the next unit is worth more than it costs

lead.text: Your answer to the pizza question was not really about pizza. You compared each slice, one at a time, with its £4 price, and you stopped when a slice was worth less than that. Economists call the extra benefit of one more unit its **marginal benefit**, and the extra cost of one more unit its **marginal cost**, and the rule you followed is the heart of the idea: do one more *as long as its marginal benefit is greater than its marginal cost*, and stop as soon as it isn't.

The figure shows the same rule with ice cream. The cones are worth £9, £6, £4 and £2 to you, and each costs £3. The first three bars rise above the price line, so each of those cones is worth buying, and the fourth falls below it, so you stop at three. The price stayed at £3 throughout. What changed was the value of each extra cone, which usually falls as you have more, because the first cone satisfies a stronger want than the fourth.

afterFigure.text: Notice that every comparison is between the *next* unit and its own cost. A total can look wonderful while the next step is a mistake, and that is the trap the rest of this lesson keeps returning to.

steps.headline: A marginal cost can rise as you do more

lead.text: A price is not the only kind of marginal cost, and it does not always stay put. Take a florist deciding how many hours to stay open late. The first late hour brings £50 of extra sales and costs £20 in wages and electricity, the second brings £40 and costs £22, the third brings £25 and costs £30, and the fourth brings £10 and costs £35. The costs creep up because later hours mean paying overtime and finding someone willing to stay.

Read down the hours and the first two each bring in more than they cost, while the third adds £25 and costs £30, so the florist stops at two. Switch to the second view, where the same benefits face a flat cost of £20 an hour, and the third hour, worth £25, now pays its way; only the fourth, worth £10, does not.

afterFigure.text: The benefits are identical in the two views and yet the best number of hours is different. The stopping point is set by **the two margins together**, and *neither* one decides it alone.

steps.headline: Following the margin makes the total net benefit as large as possible

lead.text: There is a second way to reach the same answer, and it shows what the rule is for. For each hour, subtract its marginal cost from its marginal benefit and call the result its **net benefit**. The florist's four late hours net £30, £18, −£5 and −£25. Add them up as you go and the total net benefit after one, two, three and four hours is £30, £48, £43 and £18.

afterFigure.text: The total peaks at two hours, at £48, and it peaks there for exactly the reason the rule gives: every hour up to the second added something and every hour after it took something away. So stopping where the marginal benefit falls below the marginal cost is the same thing as making the total net benefit *as large as it can be*.

steps.headline: How many late hours should the bookshop open?

lead.text: A bookshop is weighing four late hours. The method is to net each hour, open the ones that add something, and total what they add.

workedSteps.text: List the marginal benefit and marginal cost of each hour, in order.
Subtract to find each hour's net benefit.
Open the hours that add something and stop at the first that does not.
Add the nets of the hours opened to get the total net benefit.

steps.headline: The café's first three hours, net by net

lead.text: Now do the same for the café, whose benefits and costs are in the figure. Two of the lines are left for you.

workedSteps.text: Hour 1 brings £90 and costs £30.
Hour 2 brings £70 and costs £35. What is its net benefit?
Hour 3 brings £55 and costs £45.
Add the three nets to get the total net benefit.

steps.headline: A cost you cannot get back should not change what you do next

lead.text: One cost never belongs in the comparison. Suppose you have bought a £25 concert ticket that cannot be refunded, and on the evening you feel ill. Should you go because you've paid? Look at the two evenings. If you go, you have spent £25 and you hear the concert while unwell; if you stay at home, you have spent £25 and you spend the evening in bed. The £25 appears in both.

We call a cost that has already been paid, and cannot be recovered whatever you decide next, a **sunk cost**, and because it is the same under every option it cannot make one option better than another. What does *differ* is the evening itself, music while ill against rest, and that is what you should weigh.

afterFigure.text: The same goes for a business. A licence fee paid last month is a reason for neither opening an extra hour nor closing one, because it is gone either way.

steps.headline: Totals and averages can hide the hour that loses money

lead.text: A tempting shortcut is to judge the whole activity at once. The florist's first three late hours bring £50 + £40 + £25 = £115 of benefit, a little over £38 an hour, and their costs of £20, £22 and £30 come to £72, or £24 an hour. Judged as a package, three late hours look like a good deal, with £43 more in benefit than in cost.

But the decision is never whether to open three hours or none. It is whether to add *one more* to the two already open. The second view picks out the third hour on its own, and it brings £25 for a cost of £30, so it loses £5. The package only looked good because the first two hours were so profitable. **A decision about the next unit should be judged on the next unit**, whatever the average says.

diagram.alt: A bar of the florist's first three hours, £50, £40 and £25, totalling £115. The second view picks out the third hour, £25, against its £30 cost.

lessons.orientation: Choose how much of an activity to do by comparing marginal benefit with marginal cost, and ignore sunk costs.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: How many slices of pizza should you buy? Nobody settles that by asking whether pizza is worth having in general. Each time you reach for another slice you ask a narrower question, which is whether *this* one is worth what it costs, and you keep going until the answer turns to no.

That narrow question turns out to be the way to decide how much of almost anything to do, from slices of pizza to the hours a shop stays open or the number of adverts a firm buys. It also protects you from a few very natural mistakes about money you have already spent.

intro.promise: By the end you'll decide how much of an activity to do by comparing the next unit's benefit with its cost, and you'll know which costs to ignore.

recap.keyIdea: Do one more unit while its marginal benefit exceeds its marginal cost, and ignore any cost that is already sunk.

blocks.text: To decide how much to do, compare the [[marginal benefit|The extra benefit of one more unit. Met in 'The next unit'.]] of the next unit with its [[marginal cost|The extra cost of one more unit. Met in 'The next unit'.]] and stop where the benefit stops exceeding the cost, which is also where the total net benefit is largest. Averages and totals can hide a unit that loses money, and a **sunk cost** is the same whatever you choose, so it never belongs in the comparison.

recap.nextHook: Next we put many buyers and sellers in one market and ask what price comes out.

lessons.title: Demand meets supply

steps.headline: As the price rises, buyers plan to buy less

lead.text: Start with the buyers of a single product, say tubs of ice cream, and ask a simple question: how many would people plan to buy at one particular price? That planned amount, with everything else held fixed (incomes, tastes, the prices of other things), is called the **quantity demanded**. In the figure, at £2 buyers plan to buy 50 tubs a day, at £4 they plan to buy 40, and at £8 only 20.

afterFigure.text: Change the price and the plan changes, and *nearly always* in the same direction: a higher price means a smaller quantity demanded, which we call the **law of demand**. It is how sensible people behave, because at a higher price some buyers switch to something cheaper and others decide the purchase was never worth that much. The line that pairs every price with the quantity demanded at that price is the **demand curve**.

steps.headline: A demand equation gives the quantity bought at every price

lead.text: The straight line in the figure can be written as an equation, Qd = 60 − 5P, where P is the price in pounds and Qd is the quantity demanded in tubs a day. Each number in it says something. The 60 is the quantity at a price of £0, where the line meets the quantity axis, and the 5 is the number of tubs buyers drop for every £1 the price rises. Check it against the last screen: at £4 the equation gives 60 − 5 × 4 = 40, the *same* quantity the line showed.

afterFigure.text: A bigger number in front of P means buyers react **more strongly to price**. In the second view, Qd = 60 − 10P, each extra pound removes 10 tubs instead of 5, so at £4 only 60 − 10 × 4 = 20 are bought. You may have noticed that price sits on the vertical axis even though the equation produces quantity from price. That is simply the habit of the subject, and it is worth getting used to.

steps.headline: As the price rises, sellers plan to offer more

lead.text: Sellers make plans as well. The amount they plan to offer at one chosen price is the **quantity supplied**, and the relationship between price and that amount is **supply**. At £4 the ice-cream sellers in the figure plan to offer 20 tubs, and at £8 they plan to offer 40. This time the quantity rises with the price, for a reason you already know: making one more tub costs something, and a seller will make it only if the price at least covers its [[marginal cost|The extra cost of one more unit. Met in 'The next unit'.]]. A higher price makes more units worth making, and it also tempts new sellers in.

afterFigure.text: As an equation this supply is Qs = 5P. The third view shows a rule with a minus sign in it, Qs = 4P − 20, and the minus sign has a plain meaning: sellers offer *nothing* until the price reaches £5, since 4 × 5 − 20 = 0, and above that the quantity climbs, reaching 20 at £10.

steps.headline: The market settles where the two sets of plans match

lead.text: Put the two sets of plans into one picture, with demand Qd = 60 − 5P and supply Qs = 5P. At a price of £4, buyers plan to buy 40 tubs and sellers plan to offer only 20, so 20 would-be buyers go without. We call that gap a **shortage**, and it pushes the price up, since disappointed buyers will pay more to be served. At £8 it is the other way round: buyers want 20, sellers offer 40, and the 20 tubs left on the shelf are a **surplus**, which pushes the price down as sellers cut it to clear their stock.

Somewhere between the two the pressures cancel. At £6, buyers plan to buy 60 − 5 × 6 = 30 tubs and sellers plan to offer 5 × 6 = 30, so the plans match, nobody is turned away and nobody is left with stock. There is then no reason for the price to move, and we call it the **equilibrium** price, with 30 tubs as the equilibrium quantity.

afterFigure.text: The word comes from balance, and it does not mean everyone is delighted. It means only that at this price the quantity people want to buy is the quantity others want to sell.

steps.headline: To find the equilibrium, set Qd equal to Qs and solve

lead.text: The picture tells us what an equilibrium is, but with equations we can find it exactly. The equilibrium price is the one at which Qd = Qs, so we write the two expressions for the quantity, **set them equal**, and solve for P. That gives the price. The quantity comes from putting the price back into either equation, and into the *other* as a check, since both have to give the same number.

Nothing here goes beyond the algebra of two straight lines, and the only thing to watch is that the price alone does not finish the job. A market is described by a price and a quantity, so always carry the sum through to the second one.

steps.headline: Driving lessons: Qd = 90 − 3P and Qs = 2P − 10

lead.text: A town's market for hour-long driving lessons has demand Qd = 90 − 3P and supply Qs = 2P − 10, with P in pounds and the quantities in lessons a day.

workedSteps.text: Set the quantity demanded equal to the quantity supplied.
Add 3P and add 10 to both sides to collect the terms.
Divide both sides by 5 to find the price.
Put the price into demand, and check it against supply.

steps.headline: Gig tickets: Qd = 100 − 2P and Qs = 4P − 20

lead.text: Now the market for gig tickets, with the same steps. The price and the quantity are left for you to find.

workedSteps.text: Set the quantity demanded equal to the quantity supplied.
Add 2P and add 20 to both sides to collect the terms.
Divide by 6 to find the equilibrium price.
Put the price into the demand equation to find the quantity traded.

lessons.orientation: Read linear demand and supply equations and solve them for the equilibrium price and quantity.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: Who decides what a ticket, a loaf or a cup of coffee costs? In most cases nobody does. Each seller picks a price, thousands of buyers decide whether to pay it, and yet the prices of similar goods end up remarkably close together and move in step with each other. A price that nobody sets still comes to rest somewhere, and the question is where.

The answer lies in two sets of plans, the buyers' and the sellers', and in the one price at which they fit together. Each set of plans can be written as a short equation linking price to quantity, and once you can read the two equations you can solve them for the price at which a market settles and the amount that changes hands there.

intro.promise: By the end you'll read demand and supply equations and solve them for the price and quantity at which a market settles.

recap.keyIdea: A market settles at the price where the quantity buyers plan to buy equals the quantity sellers plan to offer.

blocks.text: [[Quantity demanded|The amount buyers plan to buy at one price. Met in 'Demand meets supply'.]] falls as the price rises and quantity supplied rises with it, and the **equilibrium** price is the one at which the two are equal, which you find by setting Qd = Qs, solving for P and putting the price back in to find the quantity. At any price above it there is a *surplus* that pushes the price down, and at any price below it a *shortage* that pushes it up.

recap.nextHook: Next we ask what happens to that price when buyers or sellers change their plans.

lessons.title: When the curves move

steps.headline: A new price moves you along a curve; any other change moves the curve

lead.text: Take the ice-cream market from the last lesson, with demand Qd = 60 − 5P and supply Qs = 5P, settling at £6 and 30 tubs a day. Now a heatwave arrives. The price of ice cream has not changed, yet buyers want more of it at every price they might face: 10 more tubs at £4, 10 more at £6, 10 more at £8. So the whole demand curve has moved, and its equation becomes Qd = 70 − 5P. We call that a **shift** of the curve, to be told apart from a **movement along a curve**, which is what happens when the good's own price changes and buyers simply slide to a different point on the curve they already have.

afterFigure.text: The test is to ask *what changed*. If it is the good's own price, we slide along. If it is anything else, such as the weather, buyers' incomes or a rival's price, then the [[quantity demanded|The amount buyers plan to buy at one price. Met in 'Demand meets supply'.]] at *every* price is different and the curve itself has moved. A shift to the right means more is wanted at every price, and a shift to the left means less.

steps.headline: Each cause moves one curve in one direction

lead.text: Buyers' wants change for a handful of reasons, and each has a direction. When incomes rise, people buy *more* of most goods at any price, so demand shifts right, and when incomes fall it shifts left. When the price of a **substitute** rises, meaning a good that does much the same job, buyers move towards this good and its demand shifts right: if tea gets dearer, more people drink coffee at every coffee price. A growing taste for the good shifts demand right as well.

Sellers' plans move for reasons of their own. A cheaper ingredient makes every unit less costly to produce, so sellers offer more at each price and supply shifts right, while a dearer ingredient shifts it left. Better technology and more sellers both shift supply right. Use the buttons to move between the two lists.

afterFigure.text: Notice what is missing from both lists: the good's own price. It is never a cause of a shift, because it is already on the axis, and its effect is to move us along.

diagram.alt: Two lists of causes. For the demand curve: rising incomes, falling incomes, a dearer substitute and a growing taste each point left or right. For the supply curve: a cheaper or dearer ingredient, better technology and more sellers.

steps.headline: After a shift, the old price leaves a gap and the price climbs to a new balance

lead.text: Now we can say what the heatwave did to the price. Start at the old equilibrium, £6 and 30 tubs, and move demand to Qd = 70 − 5P. At £6 buyers now want 70 − 30 = 40 tubs while sellers still offer 5 × 6 = 30, so there is **a shortage of 10**, and a shortage pushes the price up. As it rises, buyers slide up their new curve and sellers slide up their old one, until the two quantities meet again. Setting 70 − 5P = 5P gives 70 = 10P, so the price is £7 and the quantity is 35.

Price and quantity both rose, which answers the puzzle we began with. The heatwave did not break the law of demand: it *moved the demand curve*, and the higher price is the movement along the supply curve that follows.

afterFigure.text: The method works for any event. Decide which curve it moves and in which direction, write the new equation, set Qd = Qs and solve. Comparing the new price and quantity with the old ones gives the effect of the event.

steps.headline: Incomes fall in the coffee-bean market

lead.text: Specialty coffee beans have demand Qd = 100 − 2P and supply Qs = 4P − 20, settling at £20 and 60 kg a day. Incomes fall, and buyers want 30 fewer kilos at every price.

workedSteps.text: Decide which curve moves. Incomes belong to the buyers, so only demand moves.
Subtract 30 from the quantity demanded at every price.
Set the new demand equal to the unchanged supply.
Collect the terms, then divide by 6.
Find the quantity from demand, and check it in supply.

steps.headline: Incomes rise in the same market

lead.text: Now run the same market the other way. Buyers want 30 more kilos at every price, and two of the lines are left for you.

workedSteps.text: Add 30 to the quantity demanded at every price.
Set the new demand equal to the unchanged supply.
Collect the terms, then divide by 6 to find the new price.
Put the new price into the new demand equation to find the quantity.

steps.headline: A change in sellers' costs moves the supply curve

lead.text: Sellers' costs act on the other curve in the same way. If sugar gets dearer, every tub costs more to make, so sellers offer 10 fewer tubs at each price and supply becomes Qs = 5P − 10. Set it against the unchanged demand, 60 − 5P = 5P − 10, and the price is £7 with 25 tubs sold. If sugar gets cheaper, supply becomes Qs = 5P + 10, and 60 − 5P = 5P + 10 gives £5 and 35 tubs.

afterFigure.text: Compare this with the heatwave. When demand moved, price and quantity rose together; when supply moves, they go in **opposite directions**, because buyers have to slide along a demand curve that has not moved. Dearer sugar raises the price and cuts the quantity, and cheaper sugar does the reverse.

steps.headline: When both curves move, only one of price and quantity is certain

lead.text: Events often move both curves at once, and then the result depends on which move is bigger. Suppose the heatwave raises demand by 10 tubs at every price while a new factory raises supply by 20. Demand is now 70 − 5P and supply is 20 + 5P, and setting them equal gives 50 = 10P, so the price falls to £5 and the quantity rises to 45. Make the factory's addition only 10, and the equations 70 − 5P = 10 + 5P give 60 = 10P: the price stays at £6 and the quantity rises to 40.

afterFigure.text: In both cases **the quantity rose**, because both curves moved right, and that part never depended on the sizes. What happened to the price did: the *stronger* move wins, so a bigger rise in demand pushes the price up, a bigger rise in supply pushes it down, and equal moves leave it where it was.

lessons.orientation: Separate movements along a curve from shifts of it, and solve for the new equilibrium after a shift.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: Everyone knows that ice cream gets dearer in a heatwave, but look at what that sentence leaves unsaid. We have seen that buyers buy less at a higher price, so how can a heatwave raise the price and the number of tubs sold at the same moment? A higher price and higher sales together look like a break in the law of demand, yet the law holds throughout.

The resolution is that two different things can happen to a market. The price can change, which slides everyone along curves they already have, or something other than the price can change, such as the weather or the cost of growing a crop, which replaces a curve with a new one. Telling the two apart lets you say which way a heatwave, a frost or a new fashion moves a price, and, once the curves are written as equations, by how much.

intro.promise: By the end you'll tell a movement along a curve from a shift of it, and solve for the new price and quantity after a shift.

recap.keyIdea: A change in a good's own price moves us along a curve, while any other cause shifts a curve, and the new equilibrium comes from writing the new equation and solving again.

blocks.text: Ask what changed. If it is the good's own price, we move along a curve; if it is anything else, such as incomes, the price of a [[substitute|A good that does much the same job, so a rise in its price pushes buyers towards this one. Met in 'When the curves move'.]], costs or technology, one curve *shifts*. To find the new equilibrium, rewrite the curve's equation, set Qd = Qs and solve. A shift of demand moves price and quantity the same way and a shift of supply moves them in opposite ways, and when both curves move only one of the two results is certain.

recap.nextHook: Next we ask how strongly buyers respond when the price changes.

lessons.title: How strongly buyers respond

steps.headline: A price change has two opposite effects on revenue

lead.text: A stall's takings, which economists call its **revenue**, are the price of each item multiplied by the number sold. Your answer to the question just now shows two effects at work. Cutting the price from £5 to £4 means each snack brings in £1 less, but selling 90 instead of 60 means there are 30 more of them, and the second effect won: takings rose from £300 to £360.

It need not go that way. Suppose the stall also sold headache tablets at £5, and cutting the price to £4 persuaded only two more customers to buy, 62 instead of 60. Takings would fall from £300 to £248, because the lower price now applies to nearly all the same customers who would have paid £5 anyway. So whether a price cut raises or lowers revenue depends on *how strongly buyers respond* to it, and to go further we need a single number that measures that response.

steps.headline: Compare percentage changes, measured against the midpoint

lead.text: A measure of responsiveness should not depend on units. Thirty more snacks is a lot for a stall and nothing for a supermarket, so we compare *percentage* changes. Percentages have a snag, though. A price that falls from £5 to £4 has fallen by 20% of its starting value, while one that rises from £4 to £5 has risen by 25%, so the same two prices give two different percentages depending on the direction.

The fix is to measure each change against the average of the start and the end, which is called the **midpoint method**. Take a cinema ticket whose price falls from £9 to £7: the change is £2, the average of the two prices is £8, and the change is 2 ÷ 8 = 25% of the midpoint, whichever way you read it. Do the same for the number sold, which rises from 40 to 60: the change is 20, the average is 50, and 20 ÷ 50 = 40%.

steps.headline: Elasticity is the percentage change in quantity divided by the percentage change in price

lead.text: Divide the first percentage by the second and you have the number we wanted: the **price elasticity of demand**, which says how many per cent the quantity demanded changes for each 1% change in price. For the cinema tickets it is 40% ÷ 25% = 1.6, so quantity moves 1.6 times as far as price. We report the size of the number and ignore its sign, because price and quantity demanded always move in opposite directions.

afterFigure.text: The figure compares two goods whose price falls from £5 to £4. The snack stall sells 60 and then 90, a change of 40% of the midpoint against a price change of about 22%, which gives an elasticity of 1.8. Headache tablets go from 60 to 62, about 3%, and the elasticity is about 0.15. When the number is above 1, quantity moves by more than price and we call demand **elastic**; when it is below 1, quantity hardly responds and we call demand **inelastic**. Exactly 1 is called unit elastic.

steps.headline: A gym day pass rises from £6 to £10 and visits fall from 130 to 70

lead.text: Here is the whole method on one example, in three steps: the percentage change in quantity, the percentage change in price, and their ratio.

workedSteps.text: Find the change in visits as a percentage of the average of the two.
Do the same for the price.
Divide the quantity percentage by the price percentage.
Compare with 1. It is above 1, so demand for day passes is elastic.

steps.headline: A bus pass falls from £6 to £4 and sales rise from 95 to 105

lead.text: Now the same three steps for bus passes, with the quantity percentage and the final elasticity left for you.

workedSteps.text: Find the change in quantity as a percentage of the average of the two quantities.
Do the same for the price.
Divide the quantity percentage by the price percentage to find the elasticity.

steps.headline: Whether a price cut raises revenue depends on whether demand is elastic

lead.text: Now we can answer the question that opened the lesson. When demand is elastic, quantity changes by a larger percentage than price, so a price cut adds more in extra sales than it takes off every unit, and revenue *rises*. When demand is inelastic the reverse holds, and a price cut lowers revenue. A price rise does the opposite in each case, and exactly unit elastic demand leaves revenue unchanged either way.

The tickets show the elastic case: cutting the price from £11 to £9 moves revenue from 11 × 35 = £385 to 9 × 65 = £585. The bus passes, with an elasticity of 0.25, show the inelastic one: cutting the price from £6 to £4 moves revenue from 6 × 95 = £570 down to 4 × 105 = £420. The same kind of move, a price cut, helps one seller and hurts the other, and **elasticity tells you which**.

steps.headline: One straight demand line has a different elasticity at every price

lead.text: Elasticity is *not* the same thing as the steepness of the demand curve, and a museum shows why. Its demand is Qd = 200 − 10P, a straight line that loses 10 visits for every £1 at every price. Cut the price from £15 to £13 and visits rise from 50 to 70, which is 20 out of an average of 60, or 33%, against a price change of 2 out of 14, or 14%. The elasticity is about 2.3, and demand is elastic.
Now cut it from £6 to £4. Visits rise from 140 to 160, which is 20 out of 150, or 13%, against a price change of 2 out of 5, or 40%, so the elasticity is only a third.

afterFigure.text: The same 20 extra visits is a large percentage when the starting quantity is small and a small one when it is large, and the same £2 cut is a small percentage of a high price and a large one of a low price. So along a straight demand line, demand is elastic at the high prices and inelastic at the low ones, and it is **the percentages, and never the slope,** that settle which.

lessons.orientation: Measure price elasticity of demand with the midpoint method and predict what a price change does to revenue.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: When a stall cuts the price of its snacks, does it take more money or less? Lower prices bring in more customers, which helps, but every snack now earns a little less, which hurts, and the price cut on its own cannot tell you which effect is bigger.

What settles it is how strongly buyers respond to the change, and economists measure that response with a single number, the **price elasticity of demand**. Once you can work that number out from two prices and two quantities, you can say in advance whether a sale, a fare rise or a dearer ticket will raise a seller's takings or lower them.

intro.promise: By the end you'll measure how strongly buyers respond to a price change, and use that to predict whether a price cut raises or lowers revenue.

recap.keyIdea: Price elasticity of demand is the percentage change in quantity divided by the percentage change in price, and it tells you what a price change does to revenue.

blocks.text: Using the [[midpoint method|Measuring each change as a percentage of the average of the start and end values. Met in 'How strongly buyers respond'.]], elasticity is the percentage change in quantity divided by the percentage change in price. If it is above 1, demand is *elastic*, and a price cut raises revenue; if it is below 1, demand is *inelastic*, and a price cut lowers it. A single straight demand line is elastic at high prices and inelastic at low ones.

recap.nextHook: Next we ask who gains from a sale, and how much.

lessons.title: Who gains from a sale

steps.headline: Surplus is the gap between what you would pay and what you do pay

lead.text: Each friend in the question had a limit: the most they would pay for the ticket. We call that limit their **willingness to pay**. A friend who would pay up to £30 and pays £22 has gained £8 that the price tag never shows, and that gain, the gap between what a buyer would pay and what they actually pay, is called **consumer surplus**. Your answer of £11 was the surplus of the two friends who bought, £8 and £3, added together.

The third friend would pay only £20, so at £22 she stays out and gains nothing, which is as it should be, since a trade happens only when the buyer values the thing above the price. Surplus is the reason anyone takes part in a market at all, and it means that the price you pay is a poor measure of what you gain.

steps.headline: Sellers gain the gap between the price and their cost

lead.text: Sellers have a mirror-image limit. Each has a lowest price they would accept, which is what it costs them to supply one more unit, and the gap between the price they receive and that lowest price is their gain, called **producer surplus**. Suppose three people each have a second-hand chair to sell, and they would accept no less than £12, £15 and £25. At a price of £20 the first two sell, gaining £8 and £5, and the third does not, since £20 is less than the £25 they need. Producer surplus is £13.

So a sale is good news on both sides, and the price decides only how the gain is *shared*. The gain from one sale is what the buyer values the thing at, minus what it costs the seller, whatever the price. A higher price hands more of that gain to the seller and less to the buyer, but the size of the gain stays the same.

steps.headline: On the diagram, surplus is an area between a curve and the price

lead.text: A market has many buyers and sellers, so we add up their gaps. Read the demand curve as a list of willingness to pay, from the buyer who would pay most down to the buyer who would pay least. At the [[equilibrium|The price at which quantity demanded equals quantity supplied. Met in 'Demand meets supply'.]] price, each unit sold has a gap between the demand curve above it and the price line, and all of these gaps stacked together form a triangle. **Consumer surplus is the area below the demand curve and above the price**, and **producer surplus is the area above the supply curve and below the price**.

Take the ice-cream market, with demand Qd = 60 − 5P and supply Qs = 5P, which settles at £6 and 30 tubs. Demand reaches zero at a price of £12, so the consumer triangle has a base of 30 and a height of 12 − 6 = 6, and its area is ½ × 30 × 6 = £90. Supply starts at a price of £0, so the producer triangle has the same base and a height of 6 − 0 = 6, which is another £90.

afterFigure.text: In the second view sugar costs more, supply becomes Qs = 5P − 10, the price rises to £7 and only 25 tubs sell. Both triangles *shrink*, to £62.50 each, because the price has moved against the buyers and the sellers are making less.

steps.headline: Surplus in the market for driving lessons

lead.text: A town's market for hour-long driving lessons has demand Qd = 90 − 3P and supply Qs = 2P − 10, which you can check settles at £20 and 30 lessons a day. Here are both triangles.

workedSteps.text: Find where demand reaches zero, which is the top of the consumer triangle.
The consumer triangle has a base of 30 lessons and a height of 30 − 20.
Find where supply reaches zero, which is the bottom of the producer triangle.
The producer triangle has the same base and a height of 20 − 5.

steps.headline: Surplus in the market for gig tickets

lead.text: Now the gig-ticket market, where demand is Qd = 100 − 2P and supply is Qs = 4P − 20, settling at £20 and 60 tickets a day. The two areas are left for you.

workedSteps.text: Demand reaches zero at a price of 100 ÷ 2.
The consumer triangle has a base of 60 tickets and a height of 50 − 20.
Supply reaches zero quantity at a price of 20 ÷ 4.
The producer triangle has the same base and a height of 20 − 5.

steps.headline: The market's total gain is largest at equilibrium

lead.text: Add the two triangles and you have the **total surplus**, the whole gain from trade in a market: 90 + 90 = £180 for the ice cream. It is the largest gain the market can produce, and the reason can be seen one unit at a time. Take any tub up to the 30th. A buyer values it at more than a seller needs to be paid for it, so making the trade adds something. Now take a tub beyond the 30th. The most any buyer would pay is less than the least any seller would accept, so the trade would cost more than it is worth and would reduce total surplus.

Equilibrium is therefore the quantity at which every worthwhile trade takes place and *no* unworthwhile one does. Nobody planned this; the price brought it about by balancing the plans of buyers and sellers.

steps.headline: Blocking worthwhile trades destroys surplus that nobody receives

lead.text: Now suppose a rule caps ice-cream sales at 20 tubs. Every tub from the 21st to the 30th would have been a *worthwhile* trade, but none of them can happen. At the 20th tub buyers would pay £8 and sellers would accept £4, and the gap closes to nothing by the 30th, so the missing trades form a triangle with a base of 10 tubs and a height of £4. Its area is ½ × 10 × 4 = £20, and total surplus falls from £180 to £160.

afterFigure.text: That £20 **does not pass to anyone else**. It disappears, because the trades that would have created it did not take place, and that is what makes it a loss to the market as a whole and not just a transfer between buyers and sellers.

lessons.orientation: Measure consumer and producer surplus as areas on the diagram and see why equilibrium makes their total largest.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: When you buy something, who gains? You do, presumably, or you wouldn't have bought it, and the seller does too, or they wouldn't have sold. But the price is a single number that passes from one to the other, and it cannot tell you how much either of them gained. To measure that, you have to ask each side what they would have been willing to accept instead.

Measuring it needs nothing more than the most each buyer would pay and the least each seller would accept, figures that the demand and supply curves already hold, and the gain turns out to be an area on the diagram. With it we can say, for the first time, that one market outcome is better than another, and by how many pounds.

intro.promise: By the end you'll measure the gain to buyers and to sellers as areas on the diagram, and say why equilibrium makes the total gain largest.

recap.keyIdea: Consumer and producer surplus are the gains of buyers and sellers, and their total is largest at equilibrium.

blocks.text: **Consumer surplus** is the area below the demand curve and above the price, **producer surplus** is the area above the supply curve and below the price, and each is half the base times the height of a triangle. Their sum, total surplus, is largest at the equilibrium quantity, and any rule that blocks worthwhile trades removes a triangle of surplus that nobody receives.

recap.nextHook: Next, what a tax does to those triangles.

lessons.title: What a tax takes

steps.headline: A per-unit tax drives a wedge between what buyers pay and what sellers keep

lead.text: Suppose the government charges a **per-unit tax** of £6 on every gig ticket sold, collected from the sellers. Nothing about what buyers want has *changed*, and nothing about what tickets cost to supply has changed either, but there are now two prices in play. The first is the price buyers pay, which we have called P all along. The second is the price sellers actually keep once they have handed £6 to the government, which is P − 6. The gap between the two is the tax, and we call it the **tax wedge**.

That second price is the one sellers respond to, since it is what they are left with, so it is the one that belongs in their decision to supply. Your answer to the taxi question was exactly this subtraction: riders paid £17, so drivers kept £5 less than that.

steps.headline: Sellers respond to the price they keep, so the supply equation changes

lead.text: Go back to the ice-cream market, with demand Qd = 60 − 5P and supply Qs = 5P, before any tax. With a £2 tax, sellers who see a buyer's price of P keep P − 2, so **their supply decision uses P − 2 in place of P** and the supply equation becomes Qs = 5(P − 2) = 5P − 10. Demand is unchanged, because buyers still react to the price they pay. Setting 60 − 5P = 5P − 10 gives 70 = 10P, so buyers pay £7, 25 tubs are sold, and sellers keep £5.

afterFigure.text: Compare that with the untaxed £6 and 30 tubs. Buyers pay £1 more, sellers keep £1 less, and 5 fewer tubs change hands. The second view doubles the tax to £4, which makes supply 5(P − 4) = 5P − 20, and 60 − 5P = 5P − 20 gives a price of £8 and 20 tubs, with sellers keeping £4. Either way the tax is *shared* between a higher price for buyers and a lower one for sellers.

steps.headline: A £5 tax on driving lessons

lead.text: Driving lessons, with demand Qd = 90 − 3P and supply Qs = 2P − 10, settle at £20 and 30 lessons a day. A tax of £5 a lesson is collected from the instructors.

workedSteps.text: Instructors keep P − 5, so replace P by P − 5 in the supply equation, and only there.
Demand is unchanged, so set the two equal.
Collect the terms and divide by 5.
Find the quantity from demand, and check it in supply.
Instructors keep P − 5.

steps.headline: The government gains less than buyers and sellers lose

lead.text: Back to the ice cream with its £2 tax. The government collects £2 on each of the 25 tubs sold, so its tax revenue is 2 × 25 = £50. Buyers and sellers pay for that, and the cost to them is more than £50. Before the tax, [[consumer surplus|The gap between what a buyer would pay and what they do pay. Met in 'Who gains from a sale'.]] and producer surplus were £90 each. With the tax, buyers pay £7 and 25 tubs sell, so consumer surplus is ½ × 25 × (12 − 7) = £62.50, and sellers keep £5, so producer surplus is ½ × 25 × 5 = £62.50.
Together buyers and sellers have lost 180 − 125 = £55, yet **the government has gained only £50**. Five pounds of surplus has gone somewhere, and it has *not* gone to anyone.

steps.headline: Deadweight loss is the surplus of the trades the tax prevents

lead.text: The missing £5 belongs to the tubs between the 25th and the 30th. Before the tax each of them was a worthwhile trade, with the buyer willing to pay more than the seller needed. After it, the gap between what the buyer would pay and what the seller would accept is smaller than the £2 tax, so the trade no longer pays both sides and doesn't happen. Those lost trades form a triangle whose base is the fall in quantity, 5 tubs, and whose height is the tax, £2, so its area is ½ × 2 × 5 = £5.

We call this the **deadweight loss** of the tax: surplus that nobody receives, because the trades that would have produced it never take place. For straight-line curves the rule is *deadweight loss = ½ × tax × fall in quantity*, and the revenue, by contrast, is the tax times the quantity still sold.

steps.headline: Revenue and loss for the £6 tax on gig tickets

lead.text: The £6 tax on gig tickets leaves 52 tickets sold a day, where 60 were sold before. The revenue and the loss are left for you.

workedSteps.text: The government collects £6 on each ticket still sold.
The tax cut the quantity from 60 to 52, a fall of 8 tickets. The lost trades form a triangle of height £6 and base 8.

steps.headline: The side that responds less bears more of the tax

lead.text: Who actually pays the £6 on gig tickets? The law says the sellers, since they are the ones who hand it over, but look at the prices. Without the tax buyers paid £20, and with it they pay £24, so £4 of the tax has landed on them. Sellers keep £18 instead of £20, so £2 of it has landed on them. How a tax is shared between buyers and sellers, which can be quite different from who sends the money to the government, is called its **tax incidence**, and here buyers bear 4 of the 6 pounds.

afterFigure.text: Why 4 and 2? Buyers cut their purchases by 2 tickets for each £1 on the price while sellers raise their supply by 4, so buyers are the *slower* to react, and the slower side is the one left holding more of the tax. The second view makes buyers slower still: with Qd = 80 − P and Qs = 3P − 20, the same £6 tax raises the price from £25 to £29.50, so buyers bear £4.50 of it. A market in which buyers react strongly turns the split round, as the next question shows.

lead.text: In this market the buyers are the ones who react strongly to price, and the sellers the ones who react less.

lessons.orientation: Work out what a per-unit tax does to prices and revenue, then measure the surplus it destroys and find who bears it.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: When a tax is charged on a good, who actually pays it? The law usually names one side: sellers send the money to the government, so it seems the sellers pay. But a seller can raise the price, and then some of the tax lands on the customer, and which of them ends up worse off is a question about prices, and not about whose name is on the form.

There is a second, quieter question as well. A tax raises money, but it also stops some sales that would otherwise have happened, and the value of those lost sales is a cost that nobody collects. Working through both lets you say who bears a tax, how much it raises and how much it wastes, using nothing more than the supply and demand equations.

intro.promise: By the end you'll work out how a per-unit tax changes prices and quantity, measure the revenue and the surplus lost, and say who bears the tax.

recap.keyIdea: A per-unit tax puts a wedge between the price buyers pay and the price sellers keep; it raises revenue but destroys the surplus of the trades it prevents, and the side that responds less bears more of it.

blocks.text: Sellers respond to the price they keep, so a per-unit tax of t replaces P by P − t in the supply equation, and solving again gives the new price and quantity. The government collects the tax on every unit still sold, while the triangle of lost trades, with the tax as its height and the fall in quantity as its base, is the **deadweight loss**, and the less responsive side of the market bears the larger share of the tax whoever pays it over.

recap.nextHook: Next we look at rules that fix a price, and at costs that fall on people outside the market.

lessons.title: Controls and spillovers

steps.headline: A price ceiling below the equilibrium price creates a shortage

lead.text: Your answer to the ticket question used a rule that does most of the work in this lesson. A law can fix a price, but it cannot force anyone to buy or sell, so when buyers want more than sellers will offer, the quantity sold is the *smaller* of the two. A legal maximum price is called a **price ceiling**. Take the ice-cream market, where demand is Qd = 60 − 5P and supply is Qs = 5P, so that the free price is £6, and put a ceiling of £4 on it. At £4 buyers want 60 − 20 = 40 tubs and sellers offer only 5 × 4 = 20, so only 20 change hands and there is a shortage of 20 that no price is allowed to clear.

afterFigure.text: Set the ceiling at £9 instead and nothing happens at all, because the market already settles at £6, below the ceiling. A ceiling bites only when it is set *below* the equilibrium price. When it does bite, the lucky buyers pay less than before, and everyone else queues, searches or goes without: a shortage is paid for in waiting.

steps.headline: A price floor above the equilibrium price creates a surplus

lead.text: The mirror image is a **price floor**, a legal minimum price. Put a floor of £8 on the ice-cream market, above its free price of £6. At £8 buyers want 60 − 40 = 20 tubs, but sellers, tempted by the higher price, offer 5 × 8 = 40. Once more the quantity sold is the smaller of the two, so 20 tubs are sold and 20 are left over, which is a surplus. The sellers who do sell receive more for each tub, which is the reason floors exist, but the higher price comes with unsold stock and with buyers who have cut their purchases.

afterFigure.text: As with the ceiling, a floor set on the *other* side of the equilibrium does nothing. At £4 the market simply settles at £6, because no seller is being stopped from charging more.

steps.headline: A £26 floor on gig tickets

lead.text: Gig tickets again, with demand Qd = 100 − 2P, supply Qs = 4P − 20 and a free price of £20. A floor of £26 is imposed.

workedSteps.text: Find the quantity demanded at the floor price.
Find the quantity supplied at the floor price.
Only 48 tickets are bought, because buyers cannot be made to take more than they want.
The surplus is the quantity offered minus the quantity bought.

steps.headline: A higher floor, £30

lead.text: Raise the floor to £30. At that price buyers want 100 − 60 = 40 tickets, and the other two readings are left for you.

workedSteps.text: Buyers want 40 tickets at £30.
Find how many tickets sellers offer at £30.
Only 40 can be sold, so the surplus is what sellers offer minus 40. How many tickets go unsold?

steps.headline: Some costs fall on people who are not in the market

lead.text: A different problem arises when a market works perfectly well for the people in it and still harms someone else. A paint factory pays for its materials, its wages and its energy, and it sets a price that covers them. It does not pay for the fumes that drift over the houses next door. Costs like that, which fall on people who are *neither* buyers nor sellers, are called **external costs**, and because the factory never counts them when deciding how much to supply, paint looks cheaper to make than it really is.

The price tells buyers what paint costs the firms. It says nothing of what it costs the neighbours, so buyers carry on buying as though that part of the cost did not exist. Suppose each drum of paint does £9 of damage to people nearby, and ask whether the market will make too much, too little or exactly the right amount.

steps.headline: The efficient quantity counts the damage as part of the cost

lead.text: To find the efficient quantity, add the external cost to the firms' own cost, which gives the *social* cost of each unit. The figure shows a fertiliser market with demand Qd = 60 − 5P and supply Qs = 5P, so the free market settles at £6 and 30 bags, but each bag washes £2 of damage into a river. Counting it, a bag costs society £2 more than it costs the firm at every quantity, which is **the same as shifting supply by £2**, and the algebra is the one you used for a tax: Qs = 5(P − 2) = 5P − 10, and 60 − 5P = 5P − 10 gives £7 and 25 bags.

afterFigure.text: The efficient quantity is 25 bags, five fewer than the market makes. Beyond the 25th, each bag costs society more than it is worth to any buyer, so making it lowers total surplus. Raise the damage to £4 a bag in the second view and the efficient quantity falls to 20, because the more damage each unit does, the fewer of them are worth making.

steps.headline: A tax equal to the external cost makes the market count it

lead.text: If firms ignore the damage because it costs them nothing, the remedy is to make it cost them something. A per-unit tax set equal to the external cost per unit does exactly that, and it is called a **Pigouvian tax**, after the English economist Arthur Pigou, who set out the idea in *The Economics of Welfare* in 1920. In the paint market a £9 tax per drum turns the firms' supply into 4(P − 9) − 20, which is the social supply you have just solved with, so the market now settles at the efficient 48 drums.

Without the tax the market makes 60 drums. The 12 drums beyond the efficient 48 cost society more than they are worth to buyers, by an amount that grows from nothing at the 48th drum to the full £9 at the 60th, so the lost surplus is a triangle whose base is the extra output and whose height is the damage per drum. This is the [[deadweight loss|The surplus lost on trades that do not happen, or should not happen. Met in 'What a tax takes'.]] idea again, now arising from trades that should *not* have happened.

lessons.orientation: Predict shortages and surpluses from price controls, and correct an external cost with a Pigouvian tax.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: When a price seems unfairly high, the obvious remedy is to forbid it. Cap the price of tickets, of rent or of bread, and surely the people who were being priced out can now afford them. Governments do sometimes pass exactly this kind of law, and the results are often not the ones they hoped for.

A market can also go wrong in a different way, by working well for everyone in it while harming someone outside it, such as the neighbours of a factory. With the supply and demand equations you can work out the shortage or surplus a price rule creates, and the tax that makes a polluting market count the harm it does.

intro.promise: By the end you'll predict the shortage or surplus a price control creates, and use a Pigouvian tax to correct a cost that falls on bystanders.

recap.keyIdea: A price control that bites creates a shortage or a surplus, and a cost that falls on bystanders makes a market overproduce until a tax equal to that cost makes the market count it.

blocks.text: A [[price ceiling|A legal maximum price. Met in 'Controls and spillovers'.]] below the equilibrium price creates a shortage and a price floor above it creates a surplus, and in both cases the quantity sold is the *smaller* of the quantity demanded and the quantity supplied. An [[external cost|A cost of an activity that falls on people outside the market. Met in 'Controls and spillovers'.]] is ignored by buyers and sellers, so the market makes too much, and a Pigouvian tax equal to the damage per unit shifts supply to the **efficient quantity**.

recap.nextHook: Next we turn from markets to the firm, and ask how much it should make.

lessons.title: Costs and the best output

steps.headline: Some costs stay put and others grow with output

lead.text: Start with the bakery. Its rent is £60 a day whatever it bakes, and a cost that does not change with output is called a **fixed cost**. Each loaf also needs £2 of flour, so the more the bakery bakes the more it pays for flour, and a cost that rises with output is a **variable cost**. Add the two and you have the **total cost** of any quantity: at 30 loaves it is £60 + 30 × £2 = £120, and at 50 loaves it is £60 + 50 × £2 = £160.
Your answer to the question just now used those figures by spreading the total over the loaves, and spreading cost over output is the idea the next screen makes precise.

steps.headline: Average cost falls as the fixed cost is spread, then rises

lead.text: Divide the total cost by the number of units and you have the **average total cost**, the cost of a typical unit: £4 a loaf for the bakery at 30 loaves. It does not stay there. At 60 loaves the bakery's total cost is £60 + 60 × £2 = £180, so the average falls to £3, because the rent is now shared among twice as many loaves.

It cannot fall *for ever*. Take a small workshop with rent of £36 whose variable cost grows faster than its output, because a crowded workshop slows down: its total cost is TC = 36 + q². At 2 units the average is 40 ÷ 2 = £20, at 4 units it is 52 ÷ 4 = £13, at 6 units 72 ÷ 6 = £12, at 9 units 117 ÷ 9 = £13, and at 12 units 180 ÷ 12 = £15.

afterFigure.text: Two forces are at work. Spreading the rent pulls the average down, and the rising cost of each extra unit pushes it up, so the average is lowest where the two balance, at 6 units. The second view, with a rent of £144, has the same shape with its lowest point further to the right. The lower curve labelled AVC is the **average variable cost**, the variable cost alone divided by output, which leaves the rent out, and the curve labelled MC is the marginal cost that the next screen takes up.

steps.headline: Marginal cost is what one more unit adds to total cost

lead.text: A firm finds its [[marginal cost|The extra cost of one more unit. Met in 'The next unit'.]] straight from its total cost. If a workshop's total cost is £40 at no units, £58 at one and £71 at two, then the first unit adds £18 and the second adds £13: each is **the difference between two neighbouring totals**.

For the workshop with TC = 36 + q², the marginal cost at output q works out to MC = 2q. You can see roughly why from one step. Going from 10 units to 11 raises the variable cost from 100 to 121, an extra £21, which is close to 2 × 10 = 20 and 2 × 11 = 22. Marginal cost *rises* with output here because variable cost climbs faster than output does, and that rise is what will turn the average cost upwards.

steps.headline: Where is average cost lowest when the rent is £400?

lead.text: A unit that costs less than the current average pulls the average down, and one that costs more pulls it up, so the average stops falling at exactly the output where marginal cost reaches it. Here that gives the lowest point for a workshop with TC = 400 + q².

workedSteps.text: Write down the two costs we need.
Average cost is lowest where marginal cost equals it.
Take q from both sides, then multiply by q.
Average cost at that output.

steps.headline: The cheaper workshop, rent £100

lead.text: Now the same two steps for a workshop with TC = 100 + q². The output and the lowest average cost are left for you.

workedSteps.text: Write down the two costs we need.
Set marginal cost equal to average cost, which gives q² = 100. Find the output at which average cost is lowest.
Find the average total cost at that output.

steps.headline: A price-taker makes units until its marginal cost reaches the price

lead.text: Now the firm's real choice: how much to make? Suppose the firm is small in a large market, so it must take whatever price the market sets and cannot change it by selling more. We call it a **price-taker**. For a price-taker, every extra unit sold brings in exactly the market price, so its **marginal revenue**, the extra revenue one more unit adds, is just the price.

That lets us use the rule from 'The next unit': make one more while its marginal revenue is greater than its marginal cost, and stop where they meet. For a price-taker this means producing the output at which *price equals marginal cost*, P = MC.

afterFigure.text: The workshop with TC = 36 + q² has MC = 2q. At a price of £20 it sets 20 = 2q, so it makes 10 units, and earns revenue of 20 × 10 = £200 against a cost of 36 + 100 = £136, a profit of £64. At £24 it makes 12 units, with revenue of £288 against a cost of 36 + 144 = £180, a profit of £108.

steps.headline: A firm can lose money and still be right to produce

lead.text: What if the price is low? Suppose it falls to £12, and the firm with TC = 100 + q² follows the same rule: 12 = 2q gives 6 units. Revenue is 12 × 6 = £72 and total cost is 100 + 36 = £136, so the firm loses £64. Would it do better to close? If it made nothing it would still owe the £100 rent, so it would lose £100 *instead*.

By producing, the firm covers its £36 of variable cost and has £36 left over towards the rent, which cuts the loss from £100 to £64. In the short run the rent is a [[sunk cost|A cost already paid that cannot be recovered whatever you decide. Met in 'The next unit'.]], owed whatever the firm does, so it doesn't enter the choice, and **the rule P = MC is still the right one** even when it ends in a loss. Whether the firm should stay in business over the long run is a separate question.

lessons.orientation: Separate fixed, variable, average and marginal cost, and choose output where marginal revenue equals marginal cost.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: A bakery pays £60 in rent every day, whether it bakes ten loaves or a hundred. So what does one loaf cost it? The honest answer is that it depends how many are baked, because the rent is spread over however many loaves there are, and a baker who sees why will make better decisions about how much to bake than one who works from a rule of thumb.

Some costs, such as the rent, stay the same however much is made, while others, such as flour, grow with every loaf. Separating the two lets you work out what each loaf costs on average and what the next loaf adds, and from that the output that earns the bakery the most profit at the price it can sell for.

intro.promise: By the end you'll tell average cost from marginal cost, and find the output that maximises profit for a firm that takes the market price.

recap.keyIdea: A price-taking firm maximises profit by making the output at which its marginal cost equals the price.
