blocks.text: **Average total cost** is total cost divided by output, and it is lowest at the output where marginal cost equals it. A firm that takes the market price earns marginal revenue equal to that price, so it should make units until its [[marginal cost|The extra cost of one more unit. Met in 'The next unit'.]] reaches the price, and since fixed costs are sunk in the short run it keeps to that rule even when the answer is a *loss*.

recap.nextHook: Next, a firm that is the only seller and so does not take the price as given.

lessons.title: One seller

steps.headline: A single seller chooses its price, and demand sets how many it sells

lead.text: Suppose one company runs the only ferry across a river, with no bridge or rival boat to compete with it. A firm that is the only seller of a good is called a **monopolist**, and it differs from the firms in the last lesson in an important way. A price-taker had to accept the market price, whereas the ferry company faces the whole of the market's demand and chooses its own price, which is why we call a firm in this position a **price-maker**.

It cannot choose everything, though. Suppose demand for crossings is P = 50 − Q, with P in pounds and Q in crossings an hour. Ask £40 and 10 people cross; ask £20 and 30 do. The company picks a point on its demand curve, and a higher price always costs it some passengers. So its choice is still how much to supply, with the added twist that the price it receives depends on the quantity it chooses, and each crossing costs it £14 to run.

steps.headline: Selling one more means cutting the price on every unit

lead.text: Your answer to the question just now was the key calculation. A firm that sells 30 units at £70 takes in £2,100. To sell a 31st it must cut the price to £69 for *everyone*, so it takes in 31 × £69 = £2,139, and the 31st unit brings in only £39 of extra revenue. The unit sells for £69, but its [[marginal revenue|The extra revenue one more unit adds. Met in 'Costs and the best output'.]] is £39, because the £1 cut on each of the 30 units already being sold takes £30 back.

A monopolist's marginal revenue is therefore **always below its price**. A price-taker never faces this, because selling one more unit does nothing to the market price, so its marginal revenue is simply the price.

steps.headline: With a straight demand line, marginal revenue falls twice as fast

lead.text: For demand P = a − bQ, the revenue from Q units is P × Q = aQ − bQ², and working out the extra revenue unit by unit gives the rule **MR = a − 2bQ**: the same intercept as demand, but twice the slope. For the ferry, with P = 50 − Q, that is MR = 50 − 2Q. You can test it on one step. Going from 10 crossings to 11 takes revenue from 10 × £40 = £400 to 11 × £39 = £429, an extra £29, which sits between MR = 30 at 10 crossings and MR = 28 at 11.

afterFigure.text: In the figure the marginal revenue line lies below the demand line everywhere, and it reaches zero at half the quantity at which demand does. The second view, P = 58 − 2Q, has marginal revenue 58 − 4Q, which again falls *twice* as steeply as the demand line it comes from.

steps.headline: Make units until marginal revenue falls to marginal cost, then read the price off demand

lead.text: The rule for how much to make has not changed: make one more unit while it adds more revenue than it costs. What has changed is which revenue we use. The monopolist compares **its marginal revenue, and not the price,** with marginal cost, and stops at the output where MR = MC. For the ferry, with MR = 50 − 2Q and MC = 14, that is 50 − 2Q = 14, so Q = 18.

It does not then charge £14. The price comes from the demand curve at that output: P = 50 − 18 = £32. Revenue is 18 × £32 = £576, the cost is 18 × £14 = £252, and the profit is £324. The order is worth fixing in your head, because it is easy to get backwards: *first* the quantity, from MR = MC, and *then* the price, from demand.

steps.headline: Demand P = 120 − 2Q and marginal cost £40

lead.text: A monopolist faces demand P = 120 − 2Q and has a constant marginal cost of £40. The steps are the ones you have just seen.

workedSteps.text: Find marginal revenue: the same intercept as demand and twice the slope.
Set marginal revenue equal to marginal cost, and not the price.
Solve for the quantity.
Read the price from the demand curve at that quantity.
Profit is the margin on each unit times the quantity.

steps.headline: Demand P = 100 − Q and marginal cost £20

lead.text: Now the same steps for the market from the opening question, with the quantity and the price left for you.

workedSteps.text: Marginal revenue is the same intercept with twice the slope.
Set marginal revenue equal to marginal cost: 100 − 2Q = 20. Find the quantity.
Read the price from the demand curve at that quantity.

steps.headline: A monopoly sells less, at a higher price, than competition would

lead.text: Compare the ferry monopoly with a river crossed by many competing ferries. Competition would push the price down to marginal cost, where 50 − Q = 14 gives 36 crossings at £14, while the monopolist sells only 18 crossings at £32. The monopoly **sells less at a higher price**, and the cause is not greed alone: it stops where MR = MC, *short of* where price meets marginal cost, because every extra crossing would mean cutting the price on all the others.

afterFigure.text: Each crossing between the 18th and the 36th is worth more to a passenger than it costs to run, yet none of them takes place. The missing trades form a triangle between the demand curve and the marginal cost line, with a base equal to the missing quantity, 36 − 18 = 18, and a height equal to the gap between the monopoly price and marginal cost, 32 − 14 = 18. The [[deadweight loss|The surplus lost on trades that do not happen, or should not happen. Met in 'What a tax takes'.]] is therefore ½ × 18 × 18 = £162, the same kind of loss as a tax creates, now arising because one seller restricts what is sold.

lessons.orientation: Derive a single seller's marginal revenue and use it to find its price and output, then measure the deadweight loss of monopoly.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: If you owned the only ferry across a river, what price would you charge? The highest price you could imagine would leave the boat empty, and the lowest would not cover what each crossing costs to run, so the price that earns you the most lies somewhere in between, and finding it takes an idea that a firm facing competition never needs.

When you are the only seller, every extra unit you sell lowers the price you can get on all the others, so the next unit adds less to your revenue than the price it sells for. That one fact explains why a single seller charges more and sells less than a competitive market would, and it lets you measure what the missing sales cost everyone else.

intro.promise: By the end you'll work out a single seller's marginal revenue, find the price and output that maximise its profit, and measure the loss it causes.

recap.keyIdea: A monopolist's marginal revenue lies below its price, so it makes the quantity where marginal revenue equals marginal cost and charges what demand allows, selling less at a higher price than competition would.

blocks.text: For a straight demand line P = a − bQ the marginal revenue is a − 2bQ, so a **monopolist** finds its quantity from MR = MC and then reads the price off demand. Compared with competition it sells *less at a higher price*, and the trades in between, each worth more to buyers than it costs to supply, form a triangle of deadweight loss.

recap.nextHook: Next, what happens when two sellers must each guess what the other will do.

lessons.title: Strategic choices

steps.headline: In a game, what you earn depends on what the other player chooses

lead.text: Until now each firm has faced a market, and the question was how much to make. Two cafés on the same street face something different, which is each other. Ruby and Sol each choose whether to close early or open late, and what each earns depends on what *both* choose. If both close early they share a quiet evening and earn 8 each, in hundreds of pounds a week. If both open late they share the evening but pay for the extra hours, and each earns 6. If only one opens late it takes most of the trade, earning 12, while the other, who has gone home, earns 3.

A player's plan for what to do is called a **strategy**, and the table of what each player earns for every pair of strategies is a **payoff matrix**. In the figure Ruby chooses the row and Sol chooses the column, and each cell shows Ruby's payoff first.

afterFigure.text: The numbers matter less than their order. For each café the best outcome is to open late while the other is closed (12), then both closing (8), then both opening (6), and the worst is to close while the other is open (3).

steps.headline: A best response is the choice that pays most against what the other does

lead.text: In the question at the start, Alpha compared £10m with £14m when Beta set a High price, and took the larger. That is the move we call a **best response**: the choice that pays a player most, given what the other player does. Take the second game in the figure, in which two railway companies, North and West, must each choose a track gauge for lines that will meet at a junction. If both lay standard gauge each earns 5, in £m a year, and if both lay broad gauge each earns 3, but if they differ, every passenger has to change trains at the junction and each earns only 1.

If West lays standard gauge, North's best response is standard, which earns 5 against 1. If West lays broad gauge, North's best response is broad, which earns 3 against 1. So the best response *changes* with the other player's choice, and that dependence is what makes these games different from the problems of a single firm.

steps.headline: A dominant strategy is the best response to everything the rival could do

lead.text: Look at Ruby's choices one move of Sol's at a time. If Sol closes early, Ruby earns 8 by closing and 12 by opening late, so opening late is her best response. If Sol opens late, Ruby earns 3 by closing and 6 by opening late, so opening late is her best response again. A strategy that is a best response to *every* choice the rival could make is called a **dominant strategy**, and a player who has one needs no guess about the rival: opening late is right whatever Sol does.

The game is symmetric, so Sol reasons in the same way, and both open late, earning 6 each, even though both closing early would have paid 8 each. On the quieter street in the second view, opening late is still dominant for both, and the outcome is 4 each where 6 each was on offer.

steps.headline: An equilibrium is a pair of choices in which neither player gains by switching alone

lead.text: A dominant strategy is a strong condition, and many games do not have one. A more general idea asks about a *pair* of choices: is each one a best response to the other? If so, neither player can do better by changing their own choice alone, and we call the pair a **Nash equilibrium**, after the mathematician John Nash, who set the idea out in 1950. In the café game, open late for both is an equilibrium: if Ruby alone switched to closing early she would earn 3 instead of 6, and Sol would lose in the same way.

When both players have [[dominant strategies|A strategy that is the best response to everything the rival could do. Met in 'Strategic choices'.]], the outcome is an equilibrium, but an equilibrium can exist without them. In the second view the railways have no dominant strategy, yet both laying standard gauge is an equilibrium, since a railway that switched alone would earn 1 instead of 5, and both laying broad gauge is one as well, since a lone switch would earn 1 instead of 3. Nothing in the payoffs says which of the two the railways will land on.

steps.headline: Finding the equilibrium of the price war

lead.text: Alpha and Beta each set a High or a Low price. The payoffs are profits in £m, written (Alpha, Beta): High/High (10, 10), High/Low (2, 14), Low/High (14, 2) and Low/Low (5, 5).

workedSteps.text: Alpha's best response if Beta sets High: compare 10 with 14.
Alpha's best response if Beta sets Low: compare 2 with 5.
Low is Alpha's best response either way, so it is a dominant strategy. The game is symmetric, so it is Beta's as well.
Both firms set Low, and the equilibrium is Low/Low.

steps.headline: Counting the equilibria of the plug game

lead.text: Two makers of a charger must each pick a plug standard. A matching pair earns each of them £6m if both choose plug A and £4m if both choose plug B, and a mismatch earns nothing. Neither maker has a dominant strategy, so we check each outcome by asking whether either maker would gain by switching alone. Two of the checks are left for you.

workedSteps.text: Start at plug A for both, which pays (6, 6). If Maker A alone switched to plug B, what would it earn?
Switching leaves Maker A worse off, and the same holds for Maker B, so plug A for both is an equilibrium. Now run the same check on plug B for both and on each of the two mismatches.
How many Nash equilibria does the game have?

steps.headline: When each player's best move leaves both worse off, the game is a prisoner's dilemma

lead.text: Look at what the price war did. Each firm, reasoning correctly, chose Low, and each earned £5m, when both setting High would have given them £10m each. The outcome that each firm's own interest produces is worse for both than an outcome they could have had. A game with that structure is called a **prisoner's dilemma**. Merrill Flood and Melvin Dresher set it out at the RAND Corporation in 1950, and Albert Tucker supplied the story of two prisoners that gives it its name.

The trouble is not stupidity. High/High is not an equilibrium, because a firm that expects the other to stay High gains by cutting its price to Low, which earns 14 instead of 10, and the other firm knows it. So the better outcome is unstable unless something holds it in place, and that is the question the next screen takes up.

steps.headline: Repetition can make cooperation pay

lead.text: The dilemma assumes the firms meet just once, but real firms meet again next week. In a **repeated game** the same players play the same game several times, and each can now let its move depend on what happened before, which gives it a way to reward and a way to punish. The simplest such plan is **tit for tat**: cooperate in the first round, and after that copy whatever the rival did last round. In computer tournaments of the repeated dilemma that the political scientist Robert Axelrod ran around 1980, tit for tat, entered by Anatol Rapoport, scored best.

Take the cafés over three nights, with closing early as cooperating and Ruby playing tit for tat. If Sol opens late every night he earns 12 on the first night, while Ruby closes, and 6 on each night after, because Ruby now copies him, which makes 12 + 6 + 6 = 24. If he cooperates throughout, both close early and he earns 8 × 3 = 24 as well. Exploiting Ruby gains him nothing over three nights, and over four it loses him ground, with 12 + 6 + 6 + 6 = 30 against 8 × 4 = 32.

afterFigure.text: This works only while there is a next round that matters to the players, since the threat of being copied is what makes cooperating worth Sol's while.

cases.label: Ruby tit for tat v Sol always open late
Tit for tat v always Low
Tit for tat v tit for tat

lessons.orientation: Find best responses, dominant strategies and Nash equilibria in payoff matrices, and see how repetition supports cooperation.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: When two firms set their prices, each one's best price depends on the other's, and the other's depends on yours. A firm that treats its rival's price as a fixed fact has misread the situation, and one that tries to guess the rival's mind has an impossible job. Yet there is a way to reason about such a standoff that does not rely on guessing.

It begins with a table of what each firm would earn for every pair of choices, and with one comparison that you can already make: given what the rival does, which of my choices pays more? From that comparison alone you can predict where a price war will end up, and see why two firms that each choose sensibly can both earn less than they could have.

intro.promise: By the end you'll find best responses, dominant strategies and equilibria in a payoff table, and see when repetition makes cooperation pay.

recap.keyIdea: A Nash equilibrium is a pair of choices in which each player is making a best response to the other, and repetition can sustain cooperation that a one-off game cannot.

blocks.text: In a payoff matrix, a **best response** is the choice that pays most against what the other player does, and a dominant strategy is a best response to everything. A Nash equilibrium is a pair of choices in which neither player gains by switching alone, and in a *prisoner's dilemma* it leaves both worse off than cooperation would. When the same players meet again, a plan such as tit for tat can make cooperating worth while.

questions.prompt: Workshop A can make at most 60 chairs or 20 tables a week, trading one for the other at a constant rate. How many chairs does each extra table cost?
hints: Both maximums use the same week of work.
Ask how many chairs one table's share of the week could have made.
Divide the most chairs by the most tables.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 60 chairs ÷ 20 tables = 3 chairs per table.

questions.onCorrect: 3 chairs. A table uses a twentieth of the week, and a twentieth of the week could have made 60 ÷ 20 chairs.

misconceptions.feedback: 20 is the most tables the week allows. The question asks how many chairs one table replaces.
That is every chair the week could make. One table uses only its own slice of the week.
The goods trade at a ratio, so subtracting the maximums does not work. Compare them by dividing.

questions.prompt: Workshop A can make at most 60 chairs or 20 tables a week at a constant rate. In one week it makes 30 chairs and 5 tables. Where does that point lie?
hints: Work out how many tables the time left after 30 chairs could make.

acceptedIdeas: Inside the frontier
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Thirty chairs leave time for 10 tables, so making only 5 tables wastes capacity: the point is inside the frontier.

choices.label: Beyond the frontier
On the frontier
Inside the frontier

questions.onCorrect: 30 chairs use half the week, which leaves time for 10 tables. Making 5 leaves hours idle.

misconceptions.feedback: On the frontier means the whole week is used. Work out how many tables the time left after 30 chairs could make.
Beyond the frontier would need more hours than the week holds. Check how much of the week 30 chairs use.

questions.prompt: On the bowed frontier in the figure, how many machines are given up in moving from 40 food to 60 food?
hints: Only the machines column matters for what is given up.
Find the machines at both points.
Subtract the later figure from the earlier one.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Machines fall from 70 to 40: 70 − 40 = 30 machines for 20 more food.

questions.onCorrect: Machines fall from 70 to 40, so 30 machines are given up for the extra 20 units of food.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number of machines at the starting point. What is given up is the fall between the two points.
That is the number of machines at the end point. Take the change from start to end.
That is the food gained. The question asks about machines.

questions.prompt: On a country's bowed frontier, food rises from 60 to 80 units while machines fall from 40 to 0. What is the opportunity cost of each unit of food in this step, in machines?
hints: Find the machines lost in this step.
Find the food gained in this step.
Divide the loss by the gain.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 40 machines ÷ 20 food = 2 machines per unit of food.

questions.onCorrect: 2 machines per unit, which is more than the 1.5 of the step before it.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the machines lost in total. Divide by the food gained to price one unit.
That is the food gained, not the machines given up per unit.
That averages over the whole frontier. Use only the step from 60 to 80 food.

questions.prompt: Priya has 12 hours of study time. An essay takes her 3 hours and a problem set takes 1.5 hours. What is the opportunity cost of one essay, measured in problem sets?
hints: An essay uses up a fixed block of time.
Ask how many problem sets fit into that same block.
Divide the essay's time by the time for one problem set.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 3 ÷ 1.5 = 2 problem sets per essay. The 12-hour total does not change the rate.

questions.onCorrect: 2 problem sets. An essay costs whatever the same hours would have produced, and the 12-hour total does not change that rate.

misconceptions.feedback: That is how many essays 12 hours allow. Compare one essay's time with one problem set's time.
That is a problem set's cost in essays, the wrong way up.
That is every problem set 12 hours could hold. One essay uses only its own block of time.

questions.prompt: A production possibilities frontier bows outward from the origin. What does that shape show about the opportunity cost of the good on the horizontal axis?
hints: Compare how steep the frontier is near each axis.

acceptedIdeas: Increasing opportunity cost
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Each extra unit of one good costs more of the other, as resources less suited to it are moved across.

choices.label: Constant opportunity cost
Increasing opportunity cost
Falling opportunity cost

questions.onCorrect: Each extra unit costs more of the other good, because the resources moved across are less and less suited to the job.

misconceptions.feedback: A constant cost gives a straight line, not a bow.
A falling cost would bend the frontier inward, towards the origin.

questions.prompt: In a day Ana can bake 12 loaves or 6 cakes. What is her opportunity cost of one cake, in loaves?
hints: Both maximums use the same day.
A cake takes a sixth of the day, and a sixth of the day could have made some loaves.
Divide the most loaves by the most cakes.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 12 loaves ÷ 6 cakes = 2 loaves per cake.

questions.onCorrect: A cake takes a sixth of Ana's day, and a sixth of the day could have made 12 ÷ 6 = 2 loaves.

misconceptions.feedback: That prices a loaf in cakes, the wrong way up. The question asks for the cost of a cake, in loaves.
That is the most cakes she can bake. Its price in loaves comes from dividing the two maximums.
That is every loaf the day could make. One cake uses only its own slice of the day.

questions.prompt: In a day Ana can bake 12 loaves or 6 cakes, and Ben can bake 6 loaves or 4 cakes. Who gives up fewer loaves to bake a cake?
hints: Price a cake in loaves for each baker.
Ana's price is 12 ÷ 6. Work out Ben's in the same way.

acceptedIdeas: Ben
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Ben. A cake costs him 6 ÷ 4 = 1.5 loaves, against Ana's 2.

choices.label: Neither: they give up the same
Ben
Ana

questions.onCorrect: Ben. A cake costs him 6 ÷ 4 = 1.5 loaves, which is less than the 2 it costs Ana.

misconceptions.feedback: Ana is the faster baker of loaves, but speed is not the question. Her cake costs 12 ÷ 6 = 2 loaves, and Ben's costs fewer.
A cake costs Ana 12 ÷ 6 = 2 loaves and costs Ben 6 ÷ 4 = 1.5, so their costs differ by half a loaf.

questions.prompt: Before trading, making 2 cakes left Ben time for 3 loaves. After the swap he keeps 2 cakes and has the 3.5 loaves he received. How many more loaves does he end up with than before?
hints: Compare the loaves he has alongside his 2 cakes before and after.
Before, he could make 3 loaves; now he has 3.5.
Subtract the 3 he could have made from the 3.5 he now has.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: He ends with 3.5 loaves where he could have made 3, so he has 3.5 − 3 = 0.5 loaves more.

questions.onCorrect: He has the same 2 cakes and 3.5 loaves where he would have had 3, a gain of half a loaf.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the total he receives. The gain is how much more that is than the 3 loaves he could have made himself.
That is what he could have made himself. The gain is the difference between that and what he now has.
A quarter is the gap between the price and Ana's cost, not Ben's gain on two cakes. Compare 3.5 with 3.

questions.prompt: Cara can bake 8 loaves or 4 cakes a day, and Dan can bake 4 loaves or 2 cakes. By how many loaves does their opportunity cost of a cake differ?
hints: Price a cake in loaves for Cara.
Price a cake in loaves for Dan.
Subtract one price from the other.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each gives up 8 ÷ 4 = 4 ÷ 2 = 2 loaves per cake, so the costs are equal and the difference is nothing.

questions.onCorrect: Both give up 2 loaves for each cake, so neither has a comparative advantage and a swap offers neither of them anything.

misconceptions.feedback: Two loaves is what a cake costs each of them. The question asks how much those two costs differ.
That is the gap between their maximum loaves, which shows who is faster. It says nothing about how their costs differ.
Check each price: Cara gives up 8 ÷ 4 loaves per cake and Dan gives up 4 ÷ 2. Then subtract.

questions.prompt: In an hour Mira can code 4 web pages or write 8 reports. Tom can code 1 page or write 4 reports. What is Tom's opportunity cost of one page, in reports?
hints: Both maximums use the same hour.
A page uses a quarter of Tom's hour in this case; ask how many reports that could have been.
Divide the most reports by the most pages.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Tom gives up 4 reports ÷ 1 page = 4 reports per page; Mira gives up only 2.

questions.onCorrect: A page costs Tom 4 reports, against 2 for Mira, so Mira is the one who should code.

misconceptions.feedback: That prices a report in pages, the wrong way up. The question asks for the cost of a page, in reports.
That is the most pages Tom can code. Its price in reports comes from dividing the maximum reports by it.
Subtracting the maximums does not give a rate. Divide the reports by the pages.

questions.prompt: Mira gives up 2 reports for each web page she codes, and Tom gives up 4. Which division of work produces gains from trade?
hints: The one with the lower opportunity cost of a good should make it.
Work out who gives up less for a page.

acceptedIdeas: Mira codes pages and Tom writes reports
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Mira has the lower opportunity cost of pages, so she codes them; Tom's lower cost of reports makes him the report writer.

choices.label: Tom codes pages and Mira writes reports
Each splits the hour equally
Mira codes pages and Tom writes reports

questions.onCorrect: Mira gives up fewer reports per page, and Tom gives up fewer pages per report, so each should do the job they are cheaper at.

misconceptions.feedback: That gives each the job they are dearer at. Tom gives up 4 reports for a page, Mira only 2.
Splitting evenly ignores the difference in costs. When costs differ, each does better by concentrating on the good they give up least to make.

questions.prompt: A café's extra opening hours have marginal benefits of £90, £70, £55, £40 and £30, and marginal costs of £30, £35, £45, £50 and £60. How many extra hours should it open?
hints: Compare each hour's benefit with its own cost, in order.
Hour 3 brings £55 for a cost of £45. Check hour 4 in the same way.
Count the hours up to the last one whose benefit exceeds its cost.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Hours one to three each bring more than they cost (£90 > £30, £70 > £35, £55 > £45); the fourth brings £40 for £50, so stop.

questions.onCorrect: The third hour brings £55 for a cost of £45, but the fourth brings £40 for £50, so three hours is where the benefit stops exceeding the cost.

misconceptions.feedback: The fourth hour brings £40 and costs £50, so it takes £10 more than it adds.
The third hour brings £55 against a cost of £45, so it still adds £10 and is worth opening.
Opening all five ignores that the fourth and fifth hours cost more than they bring in.

questions.prompt: The café opens its first three extra hours, which bring £90, £70 and £55 and cost £30, £35 and £45. What is their total net benefit, in pounds?
hints: Find each hour's net benefit.
The nets are £60, £35 and so on; work out the third.
Add the three nets.
questions.onCorrect: The three hours net £60, £35 and £10, which add up to £105.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the total benefit of the three hours. Subtract their total cost as well.
That is the total cost of the three hours. The net benefit is the benefit minus the cost.
That is the net benefit of the second hour only. Add the nets of all three hours.

questions.prompt: The café's hours bring marginal benefits of £90, £70, £55, £40 and £30. Its marginal costs rise by £20 to £50, £55, £65, £70 and £80. How many extra hours should it now open?
hints: Compare each hour's benefit with its new cost.
Hour 3 now brings £55 for a cost of £65.
Count the hours before the first one whose cost exceeds its benefit.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: £90 > £50 and £70 > £55, but £55 < £65, so it opens two hours.

questions.onCorrect: The third hour now brings £55 for a cost of £65, so the café stops at two.

misconceptions.feedback: That was the answer before the costs rose. The third hour now costs £65 and brings £55.
The second hour brings £70 against a cost of £55, so it is still worth opening.
Opening every hour ignores that the later hours cost more than they bring.

questions.prompt: Over four extra hours the café's benefits average £63.75 an hour against costs of £40 an hour. The fourth hour on its own brings £40 and costs £50. By how many pounds does opening that fourth hour change the café's net benefit?
hints: Ignore the averages and look at the fourth hour alone.
Subtract the hour's cost from its benefit.
The answer is negative if the hour loses money.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: £40 − £50 = −£10: opening the fourth hour makes the café worse off.

questions.onCorrect: The hour adds £40 and costs £50, so it lowers the net benefit by £10 however good the averages look.

misconceptions.feedback: The size is right but the sign is not. The hour costs more than it brings, so the net benefit falls.
That is the gap between the two averages. The fourth hour has its own benefit and cost, and only those count.
That is the hour's benefit alone. Subtract its cost of £50.

questions.prompt: A student values successive hours of revision at 50, 40, 30, 20 and 10 points, and each hour costs her 25 points of other activities. How many hours should she revise?
hints: Compare each hour's value with the 25 points it costs.
Hour 3 is worth 30 points; check hour 4.
Count the hours worth more than 25 points.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 50, 40 and 30 each exceed 25; the fourth hour's 20 does not.

questions.onCorrect: The third hour is worth 30 points for a cost of 25, and the fourth is worth only 20, so she stops at three.

misconceptions.feedback: The fourth hour is worth 20 points and costs 25, so it leaves her 5 points worse off.
The third hour is worth 30 points against a cost of 25, so it is still worth doing.
Revising for all five hours ignores that the last two are worth less than they cost.

questions.prompt: A cost that has already been paid and cannot be recovered, whatever you decide next, is called what kind of cost? One word.
hints: It is the same under every option you could choose.
The word describes something that has gone under and cannot be brought back.

acceptedIdeas: Sunk
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Sunk. It is the same under every option, so it should not affect the choice.

questions.onCorrect: A sunk cost is the same under every option, so it cannot make one option better than another.

misconceptions.feedback: A marginal cost is the extra cost of one more unit, and it can still be avoided. This cost is already paid.
A fixed cost does not change with output, but it may still be avoidable. The term wanted is for a cost that is paid and gone.

questions.prompt: Demand for gig tickets is Qd = 100 − 2P, with P in pounds and Q in tickets a day. How many tickets are demanded at a price of £15?
hints: Replace P with 15 in the equation.
Work out the 2 × 15 first.
Take that from 100.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Qd = 100 − 2 × 15 = 70 tickets.

questions.onCorrect: Qd = 100 − 2 × 15 = 70 tickets a day.

misconceptions.feedback: That takes only the price from 100. The price is multiplied by 2 first.
That is the 2 × 15 that comes off the 100. The quantity demanded is what remains.
That is the quantity at a price of £0. Put the £15 into the equation.

questions.prompt: Demand for gig tickets is Qd = 100 − 2P and supply is Qs = 4P − 20, with P in pounds and Q in tickets a day. What is the equilibrium price, in pounds?
hints: Set Qd equal to Qs.
Collect the P terms on one side and the numbers on the other, leaving a multiple of P.
Divide both sides by 6.
questions.onCorrect: Setting 100 − 2P = 4P − 20 gives 120 = 6P, so the equilibrium price is £20.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the quantity traded. The price comes first, from setting Qd equal to Qs.
That is 6P, the line before the last division. Divide by 6 to find P.
That moves the constant term across the equals sign without changing its sign. A term changes sign when it crosses.

questions.prompt: At that equilibrium price of £20, how many gig tickets are traded per day?
hints: Put the price into the demand equation.
Check the answer against the supply equation, which must give the same quantity.
questions.onCorrect: Both equations give 60 tickets at £20, which is the sign that the price is right.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the price. Put it into an equation to find the quantity.
That is 6P from the algebra, not a quantity. Put the price into the demand equation.

questions.prompt: With Qd = 100 − 2P and Qs = 4P − 20, the price of gig tickets is stuck at £25. How many tickets are offered but not bought each day?
hints: Find the quantity demanded and the quantity supplied at £25.
Qd is 50, and Qs comes from 4 × 25 − 20.
Take the smaller quantity from the larger.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Qs = 100 − 20 = 80 and Qd = 100 − 50 = 50, so 80 − 50 = 30 tickets go unsold.

questions.onCorrect: Sellers offer 80 and buyers want 50, so 30 tickets a day are left over.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the quantity offered. The surplus is how much of it buyers do not take.
That is the quantity buyers want. The surplus is the gap between that and the quantity offered.
At £25 the price is above the equilibrium, so offers exceed purchases. Work out each quantity at £25, then subtract.

questions.prompt: Demand is Qd = 80 − 4P and supply is Qs = 8 + 2P. Find the equilibrium price in pounds.
hints: Set 80 − 4P equal to 8 + 2P.
Move the P terms to one side and the numbers to the other, which gives 72 = 6P.
Divide both sides by 6.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 80 − 4P = 8 + 2P gives 72 = 6P, so P = £12 and Q = 32.

questions.onCorrect: 80 − 4P = 8 + 2P gives 72 = 6P, so the price is £12 and 32 units are traded.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the quantity traded at the equilibrium. The question asks for the price.
That is 6P, the line before the last division. Divide by 6 to find P.

questions.prompt: Demand is Qd = 150 − 5P and supply is Qs = 30 + 10P. Find the equilibrium quantity.
hints: Set the two equations equal and solve for P.
That gives 120 = 15P.
Put the price into either equation to find the quantity.
questions.onCorrect: The price is £8, and 150 − 5 × 8 = 110, which matches 30 + 10 × 8.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the equilibrium price. The question asks for the quantity traded at that price.
That is the quantity demanded at a price of £0. Put the equilibrium price into the equation.

questions.prompt: The price of gig tickets rises while nothing else changes. What happens on the demand diagram for gig tickets?
hints: Ask whether the thing that changed is on one of the diagram's axes.

acceptedIdeas: A movement along the demand curve
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The good's own price is on the axis, so a change in it moves buyers along the curve; quantity demanded falls.

choices.label: A rightward shift of the demand curve
A movement along the demand curve
A leftward shift of the demand curve

questions.onCorrect: The good's own price is on the axis, so a change in it moves buyers along the curve they already have, and the quantity demanded falls.

misconceptions.feedback: A shift to the right means more is wanted at every price. A rise in the good's own price changes the quantity demanded, not the curve.
A leftward shift needs a cause other than the good's own price. The price itself only moves buyers along the curve.

questions.prompt: Incomes rise, so buyers want 30 more kilos of coffee beans at every price: Qd = 130 − 2P. Supply is still Qs = 4P − 20. What is the new equilibrium price, in pounds?
hints: Set 130 − 2P equal to 4P − 20.
Collect the terms so that the P terms are on one side, which gives 150 = 6P.
Divide both sides by 6.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 130 − 2P = 4P − 20 gives 150 = 6P, so P = £25, up from £20.

questions.onCorrect: 130 − 2P = 4P − 20 gives 150 = 6P, so the price rises to £25.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the old price. The demand curve has moved, so set the new equation equal to supply and solve again.
That is the new quantity traded. The question asks for the price.
That is 6P, the line before the last division. Divide by 6 to find P.

questions.prompt: A frost destroys coffee crops, and sellers offer 24 fewer kilos at every price: Qs = 4P − 44. Demand stays Qd = 100 − 2P. What is the new equilibrium quantity, in kilos?
hints: Set 100 − 2P equal to 4P − 44 and solve for P.
That gives 144 = 6P.
Put the price into either equation to find the quantity.
questions.onCorrect: The price rises to £24, and 100 − 2 × 24 = 52 kg, down from 60.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the new equilibrium price. The question asks for the quantity traded at it.
That was the quantity before the frost. Supply has fallen, so solve again.
That is 6P, a step on the way to the price. The quantity comes from putting the price back in.

questions.prompt: Demand and supply each rise by 30 kg at every price: Qd = 130 − 2P and Qs = 4P + 10. By how many pounds does the equilibrium price change from its original £20?
hints: Set 130 − 2P equal to 4P + 10.
Collect the terms to find the new price.
Subtract the original price from the new one.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 130 − 2P = 4P + 10 gives P = £20, so the price is unchanged while quantity rises to 90.

questions.onCorrect: The equations give a price of £20 again, because the two shifts were the same size. Only the quantity changed, from 60 to 90 kg.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the size of each shift in quantity. Solve the new equations to see what happens to the price.
That is the new quantity traded. The question asks how the price changes.
Check the algebra: 130 − 2P = 4P + 10 gives 120 = 6P, and compare that price with £20.

questions.prompt: Tea and coffee are substitutes. The price of tea rises. What happens to the demand curve for coffee?
hints: Think about what some tea drinkers do when tea gets dearer.

acceptedIdeas: It shifts right.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Right: some tea drinkers switch to coffee, so more coffee is wanted at every coffee price.

choices.label: It shifts left.
It does not move: this is a movement along it.
It shifts right.

questions.onCorrect: Some tea drinkers switch to coffee, so more coffee is wanted at every coffee price and the curve shifts right.

misconceptions.feedback: The price that changed is tea's, which is not on the coffee diagram's axis. So it changes what is wanted at every coffee price, and that moves the curve.
A leftward shift would mean less coffee wanted at every price. A dearer substitute pushes buyers towards coffee, not away from it.

questions.prompt: Demand is Qd = 120 − 3P and supply is Qs = 2P. A new factory adds 20 units of supply at every price. What is the new equilibrium price, in pounds?
hints: Add the extra units to the supply equation.
Set the demand equation equal to the new supply equation and collect the terms.
Divide both sides by 5.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Supply becomes Qs = 20 + 2P; 120 − 3P = 20 + 2P gives 100 = 5P, so P = £20, down from £24.

questions.onCorrect: The new factory moves supply to 20 + 2P, and solving gives £20, down from £24.

misconceptions.feedback: That was the price before the factory. Supply has risen, so solve the new equations.
That is the quantity traded at the new price. The question asks for the price.
That is 5P, the line before the last division. Divide by 5 to find P.

questions.prompt: When the price of a concert ticket falls from £11 to £9, the number sold rises from 35 to 65. Using the midpoint method, what is the absolute value of the price elasticity of demand?
hints: Find the percentage change in quantity, using the average of 35 and 65.
Find the percentage change in price, using the average of £11 and £9.
Divide the first by the second.
questions.onCorrect: Quantity changes by 60% and price by 20%, so the elasticity is 3 and demand for tickets is elastic.

misconceptions.feedback: That divides the price change by the quantity change, the wrong way up. Put the percentage change in quantity on top.
That is the percentage change in quantity alone. Divide it by the percentage change in price.
That is the percentage change in price alone. Elasticity compares the percentage change in quantity with it.

questions.prompt: Ticket sales rise from 35 at £11 to 65 at £9. By how many pounds does total revenue change?
hints: Revenue is price times quantity.
Work out the revenue at each price.
Subtract the first from the second.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Revenue goes from 11 × 35 = £385 to 9 × 65 = £585, a rise of £200.

questions.onCorrect: Revenue goes from £385 to £585, a rise of £200, as the elastic demand predicts for a price cut.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the revenue after the cut. The question asks how much revenue changed by.
That is the revenue before the cut. The question asks how much revenue changed by.
The sign is the wrong way round. Revenue rises, so the change is positive.

questions.prompt: When the price of a bus pass falls from £6 to £4, the number sold rises from 95 to 105. Using the midpoint method, what is the absolute value of the price elasticity of demand?
hints: Quantity changes by 10% of the midpoint; find the percentage change in price in the same way.
The price changes by 2, and the average price is 5.
Divide the percentage change in quantity by the percentage change in price.
questions.onCorrect: 10% ÷ 40% = 0.25, which is well below 1, so demand for bus passes is inelastic.

misconceptions.feedback: That divides the price change by the quantity change, the wrong way up. Elasticity is the percentage change in quantity over the percentage change in price.
That is the percentage change in quantity alone. Divide it by the percentage change in price.
That is the percentage change in price alone. Elasticity compares the percentage change in quantity with it.

questions.prompt: Museum demand is Qd = 200 − 10P. The entry price falls from £11 to £9. By how many pounds does total revenue change?
hints: Find the number of visits at each price from the demand equation.
Multiply each price by its number of visits.
Subtract the first revenue from the second.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Visits rise from 90 to 110; revenue is 11 × 90 = £990 before and 9 × 110 = £990 after, so it does not change.

questions.onCorrect: Revenue is £990 both before and after. Over this stretch quantity changes by exactly the same percentage as price, so the elasticity is 1.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the revenue at each price, not the change between them.
That is the rise in visits. The question asks about the change in revenue, which is price times quantity.
Work out the revenue at £11 and at £9 first. The change is the difference between those two amounts.

questions.prompt: Demand for a firm's product is inelastic. The firm raises its price. What happens to its total revenue?
hints: Compare the percentage change in price with the percentage change in quantity.

acceptedIdeas: It rises
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: With inelastic demand, quantity falls by a smaller percentage than price rises, so price times quantity goes up.

choices.label: It stays the same
It rises
It falls

questions.onCorrect: It rises. With inelastic demand quantity falls by a smaller percentage than price rises.

misconceptions.feedback: Compare the two percentage changes: which one is bigger when demand is inelastic?
Revenue stays level only at unit elasticity. Here quantity responds by less than price.

questions.prompt: The price of a phone case rises from £8 to £12 and quantity demanded falls from 110 to 90. Find the absolute midpoint elasticity of demand.
hints: Find the percentage change in quantity, using the average of 110 and 90.
Find the percentage change in price, using the average of £8 and £12.
Divide the first by the second.
questions.onCorrect: Quantity changes by 20% and price by 40%, so the elasticity is 0.5 and demand is inelastic.

misconceptions.feedback: That divides the price change by the quantity change, the wrong way up. Put the percentage change in quantity on top.
That is the percentage change in quantity alone. Divide it by the percentage change in price.
That is the percentage change in price alone. Elasticity compares the percentage change in quantity with it.

questions.prompt: A buyer would pay up to £35 for a cup of coffee and buys it at the market price of £20. How much consumer surplus does she gain, in pounds?
hints: Consumer surplus is the gap between willingness to pay and the price paid.
Start from her maximum, not from the price.
Subtract the price from her maximum.
questions.onCorrect: £15. Willingness to pay minus the price paid is the surplus on that cup.

misconceptions.feedback: That is her maximum. Surplus is the part she did not have to pay.
That is the price. Surplus is the gap between her maximum and the price.
Adding them does not measure a gap. Subtract.

questions.prompt: In the gig-ticket market, demand is Qd = 100 − 2P and supply is Qs = 4P − 20, settling at £20 and 60 tickets a day. What is consumer surplus, in pounds?
hints: Demand reaches zero at a price of 100 ÷ 2.
The triangle has a base of 60 and a height equal to that price minus the £20 paid.
Area = ½ × base × height.
questions.onCorrect: Demand reaches zero at £50, so the triangle has a base of 60 and a height of 30, and ½ × 60 × 30 = £900.

misconceptions.feedback: That leaves out the half. The area of a triangle is half its base times its height.
That uses the height 50, the top of the demand curve, without taking off the £20 that buyers actually pay.
That is the producer surplus. Consumer surplus lies between the demand curve and the price.

questions.prompt: In the same market, what is producer surplus, in pounds?
hints: The supply curve reaches zero quantity at a price of 20 ÷ 4.
The triangle has a base of 60 and a height equal to the £20 price minus that starting price.
Area = ½ × base × height.
questions.onCorrect: Supply starts at £5, so the triangle has a base of 60 and a height of 15, and ½ × 60 × 15 = £450.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the consumer surplus. Producer surplus lies between the price and the supply curve.
That uses the full £20 as the height. Sellers' costs start at £5, so the height is the price minus that.
That is half of the right figure. The triangle's base is the 60 tickets traded, not 30.

questions.prompt: A rule caps gig-ticket sales at 40 a day, below the free-market 60. For the 40th ticket, buyers would pay £30 and sellers would accept £15. By how many pounds does total surplus fall?
hints: The tickets that can no longer be sold form a triangle.
Its base is the 60 tickets minus the 40 allowed, and its height is the gap between £30 and £15.
Area = ½ × base × height.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The lost tickets form a triangle with base 60 − 40 = 20 and height 30 − 15 = 15: ½ × 20 × 15 = £150.

questions.onCorrect: The 20 blocked trades form a triangle with a base of 20 and a height of £15, so the lost surplus is ½ × 20 × 15 = £150.

misconceptions.feedback: That leaves out the half, or equivalently multiplies by the buyers' £30 only. The height is the £15 gap between what buyers would pay and sellers would accept.
That is the producer surplus of the whole market. The loss is only the triangle of blocked trades.
That is the triangle's height. Multiply by half the base as well.

questions.prompt: Demand is Qd = 80 − 2P and supply is Qs = 2P. What is consumer surplus at equilibrium, in pounds?
hints: Find the equilibrium by setting the two equal.
Demand reaches zero at a price of 80 ÷ 2; the triangle's height is that minus the equilibrium price.
Area = ½ × base × height, with the equilibrium quantity as the base.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 80 − 2P = 2P gives P = £20 and Q = 40. Demand reaches zero at £40, so CS = ½ × 40 × (40 − 20) = £400.

questions.onCorrect: The market settles at £20 and 40 units. The triangle has a base of 40 and a height of 20, so the area is £400.

misconceptions.feedback: That leaves out the half. The area of a triangle is half its base times its height.
That multiplies the base by the full £40 where demand reaches zero. The height is that minus the £20 price, and the area is half of base times height.

questions.prompt: Which area on a supply and demand diagram is consumer surplus?
hints: The demand curve records what buyers would pay.
Surplus is the gap between that and the price they do pay.

acceptedIdeas: Below the demand curve and above the price, up to the quantity sold
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Buyers gain the gap between what they would pay and the price they do pay. The demand curve records what they would pay.

choices.label: Below the supply curve, up to the quantity sold
Below the demand curve and above the price, up to the quantity sold
Above the supply curve and below the price, up to the quantity sold

questions.onCorrect: The demand curve shows what buyers would pay, so the gap between it and the price they pay, up to the quantity sold, is their surplus.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the area for sellers, whose surplus lies between the price they receive and the supply curve that records their lowest acceptable prices.
The area under the supply curve is the sellers' total cost of producing those units, not a gain to anyone.

questions.prompt: A £6 tax per ticket is collected from gig-ticket sellers. Demand is Qd = 100 − 2P, and supply in terms of the price sellers keep is Qs = 4P − 20. What price do buyers now pay, in pounds?
hints: Sellers keep P − 6, so use that in place of P in the supply equation.
Set 100 − 2P equal to 4(P − 6) − 20, which gives 144 = 6P.
Divide both sides by 6.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Sellers keep P − 6, so 100 − 2P = 4(P − 6) − 20 gives 144 = 6P and P = £24.

questions.onCorrect: The new supply equation is 4P − 44, and setting it equal to demand gives 144 = 6P, so buyers pay £24 and 52 tickets are sold.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the whole tax to the old £20. Sellers share the tax, so the price rises by less than £6.
That is the price sellers keep after the tax. The question asks what buyers pay.
That is 6P, the line before the last division. Divide by 6 to find P.

questions.prompt: With the £6 tax on gig tickets, the market settles at 52 tickets a day. What is the tax revenue per day, in pounds?
hints: The government collects the tax on every ticket sold.
Use the number sold after the tax, not before it.
Multiply the tax per ticket by that number.
questions.onCorrect: £6 on each of the 52 tickets sold comes to £312.

misconceptions.feedback: That multiplies the tax by the 60 tickets sold before the tax. Tax is collected only on the tickets that are still sold.
That is the number of tickets sold. Multiply it by the tax collected on each.
That is the deadweight loss. The revenue is the tax per ticket multiplied by the tickets sold.

questions.prompt: The tax cut the quantity of gig tickets traded from 60 to 52 a day. What is the deadweight loss, in pounds per day?
hints: The loss is a triangle whose height is the tax and whose base is the fall in quantity.
The fall in quantity is 60 − 52.
Area = ½ × base × height.
questions.onCorrect: The triangle has a height of £6 and a base of 8 tickets, so its area is ½ × 6 × 8 = £24.

misconceptions.feedback: That leaves out the half. The area of a triangle is half its base times its height.
That is the tax revenue. The deadweight loss is the triangle of trades that no longer take place.
That is the fall in quantity, the triangle's base. Multiply by half the height as well.

questions.prompt: Demand for gym passes is Qd = 120 − 4P and supply is Qs = 2P − 30. A £6 tax is collected from sellers. By how many pounds does the price buyers pay rise?
hints: Find the price without the tax, by setting Qd equal to Qs.
With the tax, replace P with P − 6 in the supply equation and solve again.
Subtract the old price from the new one.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Without the tax 150 = 6P gives £25. With it, 120 − 4P = 2(P − 6) − 30 gives 162 = 6P, so £27: a rise of £2.

questions.onCorrect: The price rises from £25 to £27, so buyers bear £2 of the £6 and sellers bear the other £4, because these buyers are the ones who react strongly.

misconceptions.feedback: That would put the whole tax on buyers. The price rises by only part of the tax, and sellers bear the rest.
That is the new price. The question asks by how much it rose.
That is the sellers' share of the tax. The question asks how much the buyers' price rises.

questions.prompt: Demand is Qd = 90 − 3P and supply is Qs = 3P − 30. A £4 tax is collected from sellers. How many units are traded after the tax?
hints: Replace P in the supply equation by the price sellers keep.
Solve for the buyers' price.
Substitute that price into demand.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 90 − 3P = 3(P − 4) − 30 gives 132 = 6P, so buyers pay £22 and Q = 90 − 66 = 24.

questions.onCorrect: 24 units. Find the buyers' price with the tax, then put it into demand.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the buyers' price. Substitute it into demand to find the quantity.
That is the quantity before the tax. The tax reduces trade.

questions.prompt: Without a tax 30 units are traded; a £4 per-unit tax cuts trade to 24 units. Both curves are straight lines. What is the deadweight loss, in pounds?
hints: The loss is a triangle whose height is the tax.
Its base is the fall in quantity.
Area = ½ × base × height.
questions.onCorrect: The triangle has a height of £4 and a base of 6 units, so its area is ½ × 4 × 6 = £12.

misconceptions.feedback: That leaves out the half. The area of a triangle is half its base times its height.
That is the fall in quantity, the triangle's base. Multiply by half the tax as well.
That multiplies the tax by the quantity traded after the tax, which is the revenue, and the revenue is not the loss.

questions.prompt: Demand for gig tickets is Qd = 100 − 2P and supply is Qs = 4P − 20. A price ceiling of £12 is imposed. How large is the shortage, in tickets?
hints: Find the quantity demanded at £12.
Find the quantity supplied at £12.
Take the smaller quantity from the larger.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: At £12, Qd = 100 − 24 = 76 and Qs = 48 − 20 = 28, so the shortage is 76 − 28 = 48 tickets.

questions.onCorrect: Buyers want 76 tickets at £12 and sellers offer 28, so the shortage is 48.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the quantity buyers want at £12. The shortage is how much of it sellers do not offer.
That is the quantity sellers offer at £12, and so the number actually sold. The shortage is the gap between that and the quantity wanted.
That is the gap between the ceiling and the free price. The shortage is a gap between two quantities at £12.

questions.prompt: Demand is Qd = 100 − 2P and supply is Qs = 4P − 20. With a floor of £30 on gig tickets, how many tickets are offered but not bought?
hints: Find the quantity demanded at £30.
Sellers offer 100 at that price.
Take the quantity bought from the quantity offered.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: At £30, Qs = 120 − 20 = 100 and Qd = 100 − 60 = 40: 60 tickets go unsold.

questions.onCorrect: Sellers offer 100 and buyers take only 40, so 60 tickets go unsold.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the quantity offered. The surplus is how much of it buyers do not take.
That is the quantity buyers take, and so the number actually sold. The surplus is what is left of the offer.
Adding the two quantities does not measure a gap. Take the quantity bought from the quantity offered.

questions.prompt: A paint market has demand Qd = 100 − 2P and supply Qs = 4P − 20, where supply reflects firms' own costs, with quantities in drums. Each drum also causes £9 of pollution damage to people nearby. What quantity, in drums, maximises total surplus once that damage is counted?
hints: Counting the damage shifts supply: sellers' cost per drum is £9 higher for society.
The social supply equation is 4(P − 9) − 20. Set it equal to demand.
Solve for P, then put the price into the demand equation.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Social supply is 4(P − 9) − 20. Setting it equal to 100 − 2P gives 156 = 6P, so P = £26 and Q = 100 − 52 = 48 drums.

questions.onCorrect: Counting the damage gives a price of £26 and 48 drums, 12 fewer than the 60 the market makes on its own.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the free-market quantity, which counts only the firms' own costs. Add the £9 of damage to the cost of each drum.
That is the price at the efficient quantity. The question asks for the quantity.
That is 6P, a step on the way to the price. The quantity comes from putting the price back into demand.

questions.prompt: In that paint market 60 drums are produced instead of the efficient 48, and each drum does £9 of damage. What is the deadweight loss of the unregulated market, in pounds?
hints: The loss is a triangle whose height is the damage per drum.
Its base is the extra output beyond the efficient quantity.
Area = ½ × base × height.
questions.onCorrect: The 12 extra drums form a triangle with a height of £9, so the loss is ½ × 12 × 9 = £54.

misconceptions.feedback: That leaves out the half. The area of a triangle is half its base times its height.
That is the extra output, the triangle's base. Multiply by half the damage per drum as well.
That multiplies the damage by the efficient quantity. The loss comes only from the drums beyond it, and only a triangle of that.

questions.prompt: A price ceiling of £30 is set in a market whose equilibrium price is £20. What happens?

questions.prompt: A per-unit tax set equal to the marginal external cost of an activity is named after which economist? Surname only.

questions.prompt: A firm's total cost is TC = 100 + q², where £100 is fixed. What is average total cost at q = 5, in pounds?

questions.prompt: A competitive firm with MC = 2q sells at a market price of £30. What output maximises its profit?

questions.prompt: A firm has total cost TC = 100 + q² and sells 15 units at £30 each. What is its profit, in pounds?

questions.prompt: In that market a monopoly sells 40 units at £60, while competition would sell 80 units at £20. What is the monopoly's deadweight loss, in pounds?

questions.prompt: A monopolist faces P = 60 − 2Q and has a constant marginal cost of £12. What is its profit-maximising quantity?

questions.prompt: Compared with a competitive market with the same costs, a profit-maximising monopoly…

questions.prompt: Alpha and Beta each set a High or Low price. If Beta sets High, Alpha earns £10m by also setting High and £14m by setting Low. If Beta sets Low, Alpha earns £2m with High and £5m with Low. When Beta sets High, how many £m more does Alpha earn by choosing Low?

questions.prompt: Alpha and Beta play their price game for five rounds. Alpha plays tit for tat (High in round one, then it copies Beta's last move) and Beta always sets Low. answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Round one: Alpha High, Beta Low, so Alpha earns £2m. Rounds two to five: Low/Low, £5m each. Total 2 + 4 × 5 = £22m.

questions.onCorrect: Alpha earns £2m in round one and £5m in each of the next four rounds, which makes £22m.

questions.prompt: In the plug game, matching on plug A pays each maker £6m, matching on plug B pays each £4m, and a mismatch pays nothing. How many Nash equilibria does the game have?
hints: Check each of the four outcomes: can either maker gain by switching alone?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: A/A and B/B are both equilibria: in each, switching alone drops a maker to nothing. The mismatched cells are not.

questions.prompt: A game in which each player's dominant strategy leaves both worse off than cooperation is called the prisoner's what? One word.
